name: Comprehensive Financial Feasibility Study
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool assesses the financial feasibility of a new project or expansion. It sizes the working capital and total investment, builds an annual cash-flow projection over the economic life, and derives the key appraisal indicators (NPV, IRR, MIRR, PI, payback, ROI, DSCR) plus the break-even point, with a final score out of 100.

The business question it answers: is the project worth the money invested, how much cash is needed at start-up, when will the capital be recovered, and what sales volume is needed to cover costs?

  • Before an investment decision or when applying for bank or investor funding.
  • When comparing two or more options for the same project (change inputs and compare).
  • To stress-test the project against lower sales or higher costs using scenarios and sensitivity analysis.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull nameIn plain words
NPVNet Present ValueSum of future cash flows discounted to today, minus the initial investment. Positive = the project earns more than the required return.
IRRInternal Rate of ReturnThe discount rate at which NPV equals zero, i.e. the project’s effective annual return.
MIRRModified Internal Rate of ReturnA more realistic IRR that assumes positive cash flows are reinvested at the reinvestment rate you set.
WACCWeighted Average Cost of CapitalAverage cost of the project’s funds (debt and equity); used here as the discount rate.
PIProfitability IndexPresent value of future cash flows divided by the initial investment. 1 or more = profitable.
ROIReturn on InvestmentAverage annual net profit divided by total investment.
DSCRDebt Service Coverage RatioHow many times year-1 operating earnings (EBITDA) cover the annual debt payments.
EBITEarnings Before Interest and TaxesRevenue minus fixed costs, variable costs and depreciation.
EBITDAEarnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and AmortizationEBIT plus depreciation; a measure of cash operating profit.
VATValue Added TaxHere, the tax added on top of net rent.
One-WayOne-way sensitivity analysisChanging a single variable while keeping all others fixed to see its effect.
Working capitalWorking CapitalCash needed to cover fixed costs for several months until revenue is sufficient.
DepreciationDepreciationSpreading the cost of fixed assets over their useful life; a non-cash expense.
Cash flowFree Cash Flow (FCF)Net profit after tax plus depreciation.
Payback / Discounted PaybackPayback Period / Discounted Payback PeriodYears until (plain or discounted) cash flows recover the initial investment.
Break-even pointBreak-even Point (BEP)Sales level at which there is neither profit nor loss.
Contribution marginContribution Margin (CM)Share of each unit of sales left after variable costs = 1 − variable cost ratio.
Debt serviceDebt ServiceTotal yearly principal and interest payments on loans.

Before You Start

  • Pick the currency in “Currency:” and type the beneficiary in “Entity Name:”; both appear in the results and exported reports.
  • Gather: fixed asset cost and setup expenses, expected monthly sales, staff count and salaries, rent and its VAT rate, variable costs as a share of sales, and other monthly expenses.
  • Decide your assumptions: sales and expense growth, required discount rate, income tax rate and project life in years.
  • If there is a loan, work out the total yearly instalments for “Annual Debt Service (optional)”.
  • All amounts are in the selected currency. All rates are typed as percentage numbers (10 = 10%; 30 in “Total Variable Costs (% of sales)” means 30%), except “Employee Cost Factor”, which is a multiplier (1.61).

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Fields are listed in page order. When done, click “Calculate Feasibility”. The two sensitivity fields are used after results appear, with the “Run” button.

Invested Capital (excl. working capital)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Fixed CapitalCost of depreciable fixed assets (machinery, equipment, buildings, vehicles) in the selected currency. Depreciated evenly over the economic life.150000
Setup CapitalOne-time pre-operating expenses (studies, licences, registration, fit-out) as an amount. Included in the initial investment, not depreciated.100000

Working Capital Data (Monthly)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Monthly Cash SalesExpected average monthly sales in year 1, as an amount. Multiplied by 12 to get year-1 revenue.220000
Number of EmployeesNumber of full-time employees (whole number).2
Average Monthly Net SalaryAverage monthly take-home (net) pay per employee, as an amount.30000
Employee Cost FactorA multiplier (not a percentage) converting net salary into total employer cost (social security, taxes). 1 = no extra cost.1.61 means total cost is 161% of net pay
Monthly Net RentMonthly rent before VAT, as an amount.50000
VAT on Rent (%)VAT rate charged on the rent, typed as a percentage number.20 means 20%
Total Variable Costs (% of sales)Materials, commissions and other costs that move with sales, as a percentage of sales.30 means 30%
Monthly Fixed Operating ExpensesOther fixed monthly expenses (utilities, internet, subscriptions, stationery) as an amount, excluding salaries and rent.15000
Monthly Cash ReserveMonthly contingency amount, added only when sizing working capital (not to yearly expenses).7000
Working Capital Coverage (months)Number of months of fixed costs you want to hold in cash at start (usually 3 to 6). An empty field is treated as 3; a typed 0 stays 0.3

Growth and Valuation Assumptions

FieldWhat to enterExample
Annual Sales Growth (%)Expected yearly increase in sales, typed as a percentage number.10 means 10%
Annual Expense Growth (%)Yearly increase in fixed expenses (inflation, pay rises), as a percentage number.5 means 5%
Discount Rate (WACC) (%)Minimum required annual return (cost of capital) used to discount cash flows. Percentage number.10 means 10%
Income Tax Rate (%)Income tax rate on profits, typed as a percentage number. No tax in loss years.25 means 25%
Economic Life (years)Number of years the project and its assets operate (1 to 20); also the number of years projected.8

Break-even Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Unit Selling PriceAverage selling price of one unit (product or service) as an amount; converts break-even revenue into units.6500

Additional Indicators

FieldWhat to enterExample
Reinvestment Rate (MIRR) (%)Annual rate at which positive cash flows are assumed to be reinvested, used for MIRR. Percentage number; an empty field is treated as 10.10 means 10%
Annual Debt Service (optional)Total yearly loan payments (principal + interest) as an amount, used for DSCR. Leave 0 if there is no debt.120000

One-Way Sensitivity Analysis — after calculating

FieldWhat to enterExample
Variable to AnalyseChoose the variable whose change you want to test on NPV and IRR: Monthly Sales, Fixed Costs, Variable Cost %, Discount Rate or Sales Growth.Monthly Sales
Range (±%)Maximum relative change up and down (5 to 100), as a percentage number. Five points are tested: −range, −half, 0, +half, +range.20 means ±20%

How the Results Are Calculated

Investment and working capital

  • Monthly salaries = Employees × Average net salary × Employee cost factor
  • Monthly rent = Net rent × (1 + VAT on rent)
  • Monthly fixed costs = Salaries + Rent + Fixed operating expenses
  • Working capital = (Monthly fixed costs + Cash reserve) × Coverage months
  • Total investment = Fixed capital + Setup capital + Working capital

Annual cash flows (for each year i from 1 to the economic life)

  • Revenue = Monthly sales × 12 × (1 + Sales growth)^(i−1)
  • Fixed expenses = Monthly fixed costs × 12 × (1 + Expense growth)^(i−1) (the cash reserve is not included).
  • Variable = Revenue × Variable cost ratio
  • Depreciation = Fixed capital ÷ Economic life (straight line).
  • EBIT = Revenue − Fixed − Variable − Depreciation
  • Tax = (EBIT − losses carried forward from earlier years) × Tax rate when the result is positive; zero in loss years. Earlier losses are carried forward to reduce later taxable profit.
  • Net profit = EBIT − Tax, and Cash flow = Net profit + Depreciation, plus recovery of working capital in the final year.

Indicators

  • NPV = −Total investment + Σ Cash flow(i) ÷ (1 + Discount rate)^i
  • IRR: the rate that makes NPV = 0 (found iteratively). If there are not both positive and negative flows, “Undefined” is shown.
  • MIRR = (FV of positive flows at the reinvestment rate ÷ PV of negative flows at the discount rate)^(1/n) − 1
  • PI = PV of future cash flows ÷ Total investment
  • Payback: the year in which cumulative cash flow turns positive, with the fraction of that year interpolated; discounted payback does the same on discounted flows. If never reached within the life, ∞ is shown.
  • ROI = Average annual net profit ÷ Total investment
  • Operating margin = Year-1 EBIT ÷ Year-1 revenue; Net profit margin = Year-1 net profit ÷ Year-1 revenue.
  • EBITDA (Y1) = Year-1 EBIT + Depreciation; DSCR = EBITDA (Y1) ÷ Annual debt service (shows 0 when no debt is entered).
  • Annual break-even revenue = (Year-1 annual fixed expenses + Depreciation) ÷ (1 − Variable cost ratio), i.e. the accounting break-even (EBIT = 0); Units = ⌈Break-even revenue ÷ Unit selling price⌉, rounded up. If the variable cost ratio is 100% or more it shows ∞.

Scenarios and sensitivity

  • Pessimistic: sales × 0.8, variable cost ratio × 1.1 (capped at 1), sales growth − |growth| × 50% (always worse, even when growth is negative).
  • Optimistic: sales × 1.2, variable cost ratio × 0.9, sales growth + |growth| × 50%. Expected = your inputs as entered.
  • Sensitivity: the chosen variable is changed relatively at five points (−range, −half range, 0, +half range, +range). “Fixed Costs” changes salary, rent and operating expenses together; “Discount Rate” and “Sales Growth” are changed relatively (e.g. 10% × 1.2 = 12%).

Note: the model recovers working capital in the final year but adds no salvage value for fixed assets, so results lean slightly conservative.

How to Read the Results

KPI cards

  • Net Present Value (NPV): positive = “Accepted”, zero or negative = “Rejected”.
  • Internal Rate of Return (IRR): above the discount rate is good; otherwise “≤ Discount Rate”.
  • Profitability Index (PI): 1 or more = “Profitable”, below 1 = “Not Profitable”.
  • Payback Period and Discounted Payback (years), ROI (average annual), Working Capital, Operating Margin, MIRR, DSCR, EBITDA (Y1), Net Profit (Y1), Net Profit Margin.

Project Evaluation (out of 100)

Five criteria, 20 points each:

  1. NPV is positive.
  2. IRR is above the discount rate.
  3. PI ≥ 1.
  4. Payback is shorter than half the economic life.
  5. DSCR above 1.3 if debt service is entered; if debt service is 0, the 20 points are granted automatically.
ScoreRating
80 or moreExcellent
50 to below 80Moderate
Below 50High Risk

Charts and tables

  • Annual Cash Flows: cash-flow bars per year.
  • NPV Curve (Sensitivity to discount): NPV at discount rates of 5%, 7%, 10%, 12%, 15%, 18% and 20%; where the curve crosses zero is close to the IRR.
  • Revenue vs Expenses: revenue against (fixed + variable) expenses per year.
  • Break-even Point chart: revenue, total cost and fixed cost lines at 0, the break-even units and 1.5 times that.
  • Projected Cash Flows table: Year, Revenue, Fixed Expenses, Variable, Depreciation, EBIT, Tax, Net Profit, Cash Flow (negatives highlighted).
  • Risk Analysis Data: summary of initial investment, year-1 figures and assumptions.
  • Break-even Point card: annual break-even revenue, annual units and contribution margin. The monthly fixed costs shown next to it include the cash reserve, while the break-even itself excludes it.
  • Scenario Analysis: NPV and IRR for Pessimistic, Expected and Optimistic.
  • Sensitivity table: Change, NPV and IRR (%) per point.

Export

  • “Full Word Export” (blue button): a report with cover, entity name and date, basic inputs, KPIs, an image of the charts, the cash-flow table, break-even, and evaluation and recommendations.
  • “Full Excel Export” (green button): a 6-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Projected Cash Flows, Charts, Evaluation & Recommendations.
  • You must calculate first; otherwise a message asks you to do so.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • “Total Variable Costs (% of sales)” is a percentage number: 30 means 30% (do not type 0.3).
  • “Employee Cost Factor” is a multiplier, not a percentage: enter 1 if the salary you typed is already the full cost, or 1.35 for 35% on-costs.
  • Only an empty field takes the default: 3 for “Working Capital Coverage (months)”, 8 for “Economic Life (years)” and 10% for “Reinvestment Rate (MIRR) (%)”. A typed 0 is respected (economic life is kept between 1 and 50 years).
  • Keep the discount rate realistic: your borrowing rate or best alternative return plus a risk premium.
  • Do not rely on the expected case alone: run sensitivity on “Monthly Sales” and “Variable Cost %” to see where NPV turns negative.
  • Click “Calculate Feasibility” again after any change before exporting or running sensitivity, as both use the last calculation.

Further Help

Hover over any field to see its explanation, use the side calculator (“Calculator” button) to work out a figure and insert it into the selected field, and ask the smart assistant (robot button) to walk you through this tool’s steps.

name: Comprehensive Restaurant Cost Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates a restaurant’s or café’s monthly revenue, costs and profit from customer numbers and the average bill. It breaks down fixed and variable costs, then gives the break-even point, payback period, a restaurant health score and a capacity/occupancy analysis, plus a Monte Carlo simulation and a market value estimate.

The business question it answers: is the restaurant profitable at current figures, how many customers a month does it need to cover its costs, and which cost line is above accepted industry levels?

  • When planning to open a new restaurant or café.
  • To review an existing restaurant and spot high cost lines.
  • Before changing prices or rent or expanding delivery, to see the effect on profit.
  • To estimate the restaurant’s value for a sale or a new partner.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull nameIn plain words
VATValue Added TaxSales tax; here it is only recorded in the report.
Food CostFood Cost RatioFood cost ÷ revenue; one of the key restaurant indicators.
Labor CostLabor Cost RatioSalaries after burden ÷ revenue.
Rent RatioRent-to-Revenue RatioRent ÷ revenue.
Net ProfitNet Profit MarginNet profit ÷ revenue.
KPIKey Performance IndicatorsThe main figures used to judge performance.
Fixed costsFixed CostsCosts that do not change with customer numbers (rent, salaries, bills...).
Variable costsVariable CostsCosts that rise with sales (food, drinks, packaging, commission, waste).
Contribution marginContribution Margin (CM)Revenue minus variable costs; what is left to cover fixed costs and profit.
Break-even pointBreak-even Point (BEP)Revenue or customer count that covers all costs with no profit or loss.
Margin of safetyMargin of Safety (MOS)How far revenue can fall before reaching break-even.
Operating leverageDegree of Operating Leverage (DOL)Contribution margin ÷ profit before tax; the higher it is, the more profit reacts to sales changes.
Shutdown pointShutdown PointWhen the average bill does not even cover the variable cost per customer.
Monte CarloMonte Carlo SimulationRunning 1,000 random cases of customers, bill and costs to see how much profit can swing.
Worst 5% / Best 5%5th / 95th percentileProfit below which only 5% of cases fall / above which only 5% fall.
Sector multipleSector MultipleA number multiplied by annual profit to estimate the sale price.
Employee burdenEmployee BurdenExtra costs on top of net salary (social security, taxes).
OccupancyOccupancy RateActual customers ÷ maximum daily customer capacity.

Before You Start

  • Pick the currency in “Currency:” and type the beneficiary in “Entity Name:”; both appear in the results and reports.
  • Gather: average daily customers and average bill (including VAT), monthly working days, all fixed monthly expenses, food, drink, packaging, delivery and waste ratios, and the opening cost.
  • For capacity analysis: number of tables and seats, session length and opening hours (open the “Location Analysis” section by clicking it).
  • All rates are typed as percentage numbers (30 = 30%); all amounts are monthly in the selected currency except “Initial Investment”.

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Fill in the groups in order, then click “Calculate Costs & Profits”. Once results appear, you can enter a “Sector Multiple” and click “Calculate”, and open “Advanced Analytics” to run the Monte Carlo simulation.

Basic Information

FieldWhat to enterExample
Daily CustomersAverage number of customers (bills) per working day, dine-in and delivery combined.50
Average BillAverage amount paid per customer including VAT, in the selected currency.15
Working DaysNumber of working days per month. Empty or 0 is treated as 26.26

Monthly Fixed Costs

FieldWhat to enterExample
RentMonthly rent of the premises, as an amount.3500
Salaries (Net)Total monthly net salaries of all staff, as an amount (not one person’s salary).8000
Employee Burden FactorExtra on-costs above net salaries (social security, taxes, benefits), as a percentage number from 0 to 200.35 adds 35% to salaries
UtilitiesMonthly electricity, water and gas bills, as an amount.1000
InternetMonthly internet and telecom cost, as an amount.200
MaintenanceMonthly maintenance and cleaning supplies, as an amount.300
MarketingMonthly marketing and advertising budget, as an amount.500
Other FixedAny other fixed monthly costs (subscriptions, software, accountant), as an amount.200

Variable Costs (% of Revenue)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Food Cost %Food ingredient cost as a share of food sales only, as a percentage number.30 means 30%
Food share of sales %Food sales as a share of net sales; the rest is drinks.70 means 70%
Drink Cost %Beverage cost as a share of drink sales (assumed to be 30% of revenue), as a percentage number.20 means 20%
Packaging %Packaging cost as a share of total revenue, as a percentage number.5 means 5%
Delivery Commission %Commission charged by delivery apps/partners on delivery sales, as a percentage number.15 means 15%
Delivery Sales %Share of total revenue that comes from delivery, as a percentage number. The delivery commission applies only to this part.30 means 30%
Waste %Waste and spoilage as a share of food and drink cost (0 to 20), as a percentage number.3 means 3%

Taxes and Initial Investment

FieldWhat to enterExample
VAT %VAT rate included in the bill, as a percentage number; it is removed to get net sales (net = gross ÷ (1 + VAT)).20 means 20%
Income Tax %Tax rate on profit before tax; not applied to losses.25 means 25%
Number of employeesHeadcount, used for revenue per employee.4
Initial InvestmentTotal one-off spending to open the restaurant (fit-out, equipment, décor, licences) as an amount; used for the payback period.50000

Location Analysis (collapsible section)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Daily Foot TrafficEstimated number of passers-by in front of the site per day. Used to estimate potential customers from the location.2000
Entry Rate %Share of passers-by who walk in, as a percentage number.5 means 5%
Purchase Rate %Share of those who enter and actually buy, as a percentage number.70 means 70%
Number of TablesNumber of dining tables. Together with seats, sets maximum capacity and occupancy.12
Seats per TableAverage number of seats per table. Empty or 0 is treated as 4.4
Session Duration (min)Average time a customer stays, in minutes (10 or more). Empty is treated as 60.60
Daily Operating HoursOpening hours per day. Empty or 0 is treated as 10.14

Market Value Estimate (after calculating)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Sector MultipleHow many times annual profit a similar restaurant sells for (1 to 10); then click “Calculate”. Empty is treated as 3.3

How the Results Are Calculated

Revenue and costs (monthly)

  • Monthly customers = Daily customers × Working days; Gross sales = Monthly customers × Average bill (VAT included); Net revenue = Gross sales ÷ (1 + VAT). All ratios below use net revenue.
  • Salaries after burden = Net salaries × (1 + Employee burden)
  • Fixed costs = Rent + Salaries after burden + Utilities + Internet + Maintenance + Marketing + Other
  • Net revenue is split by the “Food share of sales” field (default 70%). Food cost = Revenue × Food share × Food cost %, Drink cost = Revenue × (1 − Food share) × Drink cost %; Material cost ratio = (Food + Drink cost) ÷ Net revenue
  • Packaging = Revenue × Packaging %; Delivery commission = Revenue × Delivery sales % × Delivery commission %; Waste = (Food cost + Drink cost) × Waste %
  • Profit before tax = Revenue − Fixed − Variable; Income tax = Profit before tax × Income tax rate (editable field, default 25%) on positive profit only; Net profit = Profit before tax − Tax
  • Profit margin = Net profit ÷ Revenue × 100

Break-even, payback and indicators

  • CM ratio = (Revenue − Variable) ÷ Revenue; Break-even revenue = Fixed ÷ CM ratio; Break-even customers (monthly) = ⌈Fixed ÷ (Net bill × CM ratio)⌉, rounded up; ∞ when the margin ≤ 0
  • Payback (years) = Initial investment ÷ (Net profit × 12); if profit is zero or negative there is no payback.
  • Margin of safety = (Revenue − Break-even revenue) ÷ Revenue × 100
  • Operating leverage = Contribution margin ÷ Profit before tax (computed only when profit is positive; otherwise “Undefined”).
  • Max capacity (customers/day) = Tables × Seats per table × (Operating hours × 60 ÷ Session minutes); Occupancy = Daily customers ÷ Max capacity × 100
  • Shutdown point: risk of temporary shutdown if the average bill is below the average variable cost per customer.
  • Efficiency: Per Seat = Revenue ÷ Seats; Per Employee = Revenue ÷ Number of employees (from the employees field).
  • Market value = Monthly net profit × 12 × Sector multiple

Scenarios and Monte Carlo

  • Profitability Sensitivity Analysis: Optimistic = customers × 1.4, Realistic = × 1.0, Pessimistic = × 0.6, with fixed costs and ratios unchanged.
  • Monte Carlo: 1,000 runs; customers between 70% and 130% of input, bill between 85% and 115%, food and drink cost ±10%. Shown: Mean, Worst 5%, Best 5% and Profit Probability (share of profitable runs). Results vary slightly on each run because they are random.

How to Read the Results

Cards and alerts

  • Cards: Revenue, Fixed Costs, Variable Costs, Net Profit (Profitable / Losing / Neutral), Profit Margin.
  • Smart alerts appear when: food cost is above 35% of revenue; labor above 30%; waste above 5%; profit margin below 10% while profitable; the project is losing; occupancy below 30%; margin of safety below 10% while profitable. If none apply, “All indicators look good” is shown.

Restaurant Health Score (out of 100)

Four indicators, each worth up to 25 points and at least 10:

IndicatorGood (25)Average (20)Otherwise (10)
Food Cost (food cost ÷ revenue)30% or lessup to 35%above 35%: High
Labor Cost (salaries after burden ÷ revenue)25% or lessup to 30%above 30%: High
Rent Ratio (rent ÷ revenue)8% or lessup to 12%above 12%: High
Net Profit (profit margin)15% or more10% or morebelow 10%: Poor
ScoreStatus
80 or moreExcellent
60 to below 80Good
Below 60Poor

Other sections

  • Cost Distribution (pie chart) and Break-even Point (revenue line vs total cost line by number of customers).
  • Monthly Cost Breakdown: each line with its value and share of revenue.
  • Investment Payback Period in years and months.
  • Margin of Safety: the higher, the further from a loss; below 10% is tight.
  • Operating Leverage: a value of 3, for example, means a 10% sales change moves profit by about 30%.
  • Occupancy below 30% means unused capacity; this is general guidance alongside the alert above.

Export

  • “Full Word Export” (blue button): a report with cover, KPIs, the cost distribution and break-even charts, cost breakdown, break-even, payback period, and margin of safety and occupancy.
  • “Full Excel Export” (green button): a 5-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs, KPIs, Cost Breakdown, Charts.
  • Calculate first before exporting.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • “Salaries (Net)” is the total monthly pay of all staff, not one person’s salary.
  • Enter the “Average Bill” as the customer pays it, including VAT; the tool removes VAT using the VAT field. If your prices exclude VAT, enter 0 in the VAT field.
  • Food and drink costs use the “Food share of sales” field (default 70%); set it to your actual mix.
  • The foot traffic, entry rate and purchase rate fields do not currently change the displayed results; use them as a cross-check against “Daily Customers”.
  • Run Monte Carlo more than once; if the profit probability is below half, revisit prices or fixed costs.
  • Recalculate after any change before exporting or computing the market value.

Further Help

Hover over any field to see its explanation, use the side calculator (“Calculator” button) to work out a figure and insert it into the selected field, and ask the smart assistant (robot button) to walk you through this tool’s steps.

name: Advanced Technical Feasibility Study for Restaurants
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool assesses a restaurant site and project from both the technical and the financial side: space allocation and seat density, whether the electricity supply can carry the kitchen equipment, water and ventilation, and then capacity, monthly revenue and costs, profit after depreciation, break-even and payback period.

The business question it answers: is this site technically fit for the planned restaurant, and is the capacity enough to earn a profit that recovers the investment in a reasonable time? It gives a technical score and a financial score, each out of 100.

  • When comparing candidate sites before signing a lease.
  • When planning the kitchen equipment list and checking whether power and space are sufficient.
  • Before seeking finance, to present a complete investment and profitability estimate.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull nameIn plain words
Prime CostPrime CostFood cost + labour cost; the key restaurant cost indicator, shown as a share of revenue.
kWKilowattUnit of an appliance’s electrical power.
Amps (A)AmpereUnit of electrical current; site capacity is measured in it.
m²Square metreUnit of area.
KPIKey Performance IndicatorsThe main figures used to judge the project.
Seat densitySeat DensityDining-room area available per seat, in m².
Table turnoverTable Turnover RateHow many times a seat is filled per day.
OccupancyOccupancy RateShare of maximum capacity actually used.
DepreciationDepreciationSpreading equipment cost over the months of its useful life.
Contribution per mealContribution per MealMeal price minus its food cost; what is left to cover salaries and fixed costs.
Break-even pointBreak-even Point (BEP)Monthly meals or revenue that cover costs with no profit or loss.
Payback periodPayback PeriodMonths needed to recover total investment from monthly profit.
Working capitalWorking CapitalCash buffer to cover expenses in the first months.
Margin of safetyMargin of Safety (MOS)How far expected revenue exceeds break-even revenue (shown in the reports).

Before You Start

  • Pick the currency in “Currency:” and type the beneficiary in “Entity Name:”; both appear in the results and reports.
  • Gather site data: total area, planned kitchen share, electrical capacity in amps (from the meter or supply contract), and the state of water and ventilation.
  • Prepare the main equipment list with each item’s power in kW (from the rating plate), price and footprint.
  • Prepare operating estimates: seats, daily turnover, occupancy, meal price, food cost, staff and salaries, rent and other expenses, then the establishment costs.
  • Rates are typed as percentage numbers (35 = 35%); monthly and one-time amounts are in the selected currency.

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Fill in the groups in order, then click “Calculate Technical Study”. An instant alert appears under the equipment list if its power demand exceeds the site capacity.

Scope & Specifications

FieldWhat to enterExample
Kitchen TypeChoose the main cuisine style (Fast Food, Fine Dining, Eastern, Italian, Grill, Seafood, Café). Descriptive for the report only; does not change the calculations.Grill / BBQ
Number of SeatsTotal seating capacity. Drives customer capacity, seat density and revenue.50
Service ModelHow service is delivered (Table Service, Self-Service, Delivery Only, Mixed). Descriptive for the report only; does not change the calculations.Table Service
Daily Operating HoursOpening hours per day (1 to 24). Descriptive for the report only; does not change the calculations.12
Operating ShiftsNumber of daily operating periods (single, two, multiple). Descriptive for the report only; does not change the calculations.Two shifts (Lunch & Dinner)

Location Analysis

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total Area (m²)Total floor area of the restaurant in square metres (20 or more).150
Kitchen Area Ratio (%)Kitchen area as a share of total area, as a percentage number from 20 to 60.35 means 35%
Electrical Capacity (Amps)Available site electrical capacity in amps (50 or more), compared with equipment needs.200
Water SupplyHow suitable the water supply is: “Yes – Suitable” 15 technical points, “Needs Development” 5, “No – Unsuitable” 0.Yes – Suitable
Ventilation SystemHow suitable ventilation and kitchen extraction are: “Yes – Suitable” 15 points, “Needs Development” 5, “No – Unsuitable” 0.Needs Development
Delivery AccessibilityHow easily supplies and delivery reach the site (Excellent, Moderate, Difficult). Descriptive for the report only; does not change the calculations.Moderate

Equipment Requirements (rows added with “➕ Add Equipment”)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Equipment nameName of the item (oven, fridge, grill...). A row without a name is ignored in all calculations.Pizza oven
Power (kW)Electrical power of the item in kilowatts, converted to amps at 220 V.5.5
CostPurchase price of the item in the selected currency; added to investment and depreciated over equipment life.12000
Space (m²)Floor space the item takes in the kitchen, in square metres.1.5

Production Capacity & Operational Efficiency

FieldWhat to enterExample
Table Turnover RateHow many times each seat is filled per day. The tool multiplies it by seats to get maximum daily capacity.2
Peak Hours per DayNumber of peak hours per day (1 to 12). Descriptive for the report only; does not change the calculations.4
Expected Occupancy Rate %Expected share of maximum capacity actually filled, as a percentage number from 10 to 100.70 means 70%
Average Meal PriceAverage spend per customer, as an amount in the selected currency.50
Food Cost (%)Ingredient cost as a share of the meal price, as a percentage number from 10 to 80.30 means 30%
Number of EmployeesTotal staff count (kitchen and front of house).6
Average Monthly SalaryAverage monthly cost per employee, as an amount; include on-costs and insurance if any.2000
Monthly RentMonthly rent of the restaurant, as an amount.4000
Other Operating ExpensesOther fixed monthly expenses (power, water, marketing, maintenance), as an amount.2000
Equipment Life (years)Years the equipment will be used (1 to 30), for monthly depreciation.10

Establishment Costs (One-time)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Fit-out & ConstructionOne-time cost of fit-out, décor and construction works, as an amount.50000
Licenses & FeesOne-time licence, registration and permit fees, as an amount.5000
Working Capital (3 months)Cash buffer to cover the first 3 months of expenses, as an amount; included in total investment.15000
Working days per monthDays the restaurant opens each month (1 to 31); daily meals are multiplied by it.26

Note: only an empty numeric field takes its default (e.g. rent 4,000, other operating expenses 2,000, fit-out 50,000, licences 5,000, working capital 15,000); a typed 0 is calculated as zero.

How the Results Are Calculated

Space and electricity

  • Kitchen area = Total area × Kitchen ratio; Dining area = (Total area − Kitchen) × 0.75 (25% for aisles and services).
  • Seat density = Dining area ÷ Seats (m² per seat).
  • Required amps = Total equipment power (kW) × 1000 ÷ 220.

Capacity, revenue and costs (monthly)

  • Max daily customers = Seats × Turnover rate; Actual daily customers = Max × Occupancy
  • Monthly revenue = Actual daily customers × Average meal price × Working days per month (default 26).
  • Food cost = Revenue × Food cost %; Salaries = Employees × Average salary; Fixed costs = Rent + Other operating expenses
  • Monthly depreciation = (Total equipment cost + Fit-out & construction) ÷ (Equipment life × 12), straight-line
  • Net profit (after depreciation) = Revenue − Food cost − Salaries − Fixed − Depreciation (no taxes are applied).
  • Total investment = Fit-out & construction + Licences + Equipment cost + Working capital

Indicators

  • Contribution per meal = Meal price × (1 − Food cost %); Break-even meals = ⌈(Fixed + Salaries + Depreciation) ÷ Contribution per meal⌉, rounded up (accounting break-even); Break-even revenue = Break-even meals × Meal price
  • Prime Cost % = (Food cost + Salaries) ÷ Revenue × 100
  • Payback (months) = Total investment ÷ Monthly cash profit before depreciation (depreciation is not a cash outflow); ∞ is shown if profit is zero or negative.
  • Risk scenario: revenue × 0.8 (20% decline) with salaries, fixed costs and depreciation unchanged.

How to Read the Results

Cards and charts

  • Four cards: Monthly Revenue, Net Profit (after depreciation) with “Profitable” or “Losing”, Break-even Revenue, and Payback Period in months.
  • Financial performance chart: Revenue, Food Cost, Salaries, Fixed Costs, Net Profit.
  • Risk chart: net profit under “Normal” versus a “20% Decline” in revenue.

Warnings

  • Seat density below 1.2 m² per seat: too many seats for the space.
  • Seats ÷ employees below 8: staff count is high relative to seats.
  • Prime Cost above 65%.
  • Net profit after depreciation is negative: the project is loss-making.
  • Fixed costs below 15% of revenue: very low (check they are complete).
  • Labour cost below 15% of revenue: very low.
  • Investment per seat above 5,000: high investment per seat.

Technical score (out of 100)

ItemPoints
ElectricitySite capacity ≥ 1.2 × required: 40; ≥ required: 30; ≥ 0.8 × required: 15; lower: 5
Water SupplyYes – Suitable: 15; Needs Development: 5; No – Unsuitable: 0
Ventilation SystemYes – Suitable: 15; Needs Development: 5; No – Unsuitable: 0
Seat density1.2 to 1.8 m²/seat: 15; 1.0 to below 1.2, or above 1.8 up to 2.2: 8; otherwise: 0
Equipment space≤ 50% of kitchen area: 15; ≤ 70%: 8; more: 0

Financial score (out of 100)

ItemPoints
Prime Cost %≤ 55%: 30; ≤ 65%: 20; ≤ 75%: 10; more: 0
Profit margin (only if profitable)≥ 20%: 30; ≥ 10%: 20; ≥ 5%: 15; lower: 10
Payback (if profitable)≤ 12 months: 20; ≤ 24: 15; ≤ 36: 10; more: 5. If loss-making, 10 points are deducted (minimum 0)
Break-even meals vs maximum monthly capacity (seats × turnover × 26)≤ 50%: 20; ≤ 70%: 15; ≤ 90%: 10; ≤ 100%: 5; more: 0
Score (technical or financial)Rating
85 or moreExcellent
70 to below 85Good
50 to below 70Average
Below 50Poor

Export

  • “Full Word Export” (blue button): a report with cover, basic inputs, equipment table, key performance indicators, warnings, the financial-performance and risk charts, and project evaluation and recommendations.
  • “Full Excel Export” (green button): a 6-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, KPIs, Financial Summary, Charts, Evaluation & Recommendations.
  • Calculate first before exporting.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • Give every equipment row a name; a row without a name is not counted in power, cost or space, and with no equipment at all the electricity and equipment-space items receive full points automatically.
  • “Table Turnover Rate” is treated as how many times a seat fills over the whole day, even though the field hint mentions the peak hour; enter the daily turnover.
  • No on-cost is added to “Average Monthly Salary”; enter the full cost per employee.
  • Enter your actual opening days in “Working days per month” (default 26).
  • Kitchen type, service model, operating hours, shifts, peak hours and delivery accessibility appear in the report only and do not change the scores.
  • Do not enter 0 in financial fields; 0 is replaced by the default value.

Further Help

Hover over any field to see its explanation, use the side calculator (“Calculator” button) to work out a figure and insert it into the selected field, and ask the smart assistant (robot button) to walk you through this tool’s steps.

name: Comprehensive Marketing Feasibility Study
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool tests the marketing feasibility of a project or product before you spend money on it: will the proposed marketing channels bring enough customers and revenue to cover the marketing budget, and what does it cost to acquire a customer compared with what that customer is worth over the loyalty period?

It combines market data (TAM, SAM, SOM and growth), the target audience, competitors, the marketing mix, marketing channels with their budgets, and purchase behavior, then calculates annual revenue, marketing costs, marketing contribution, CAC, LTV, ROAS and break-even customers, with warnings, strategic guidance and a market attractiveness score out of 10.

  • Before launching a new restaurant, shop or service, to check whether the marketing plan makes sense.
  • When comparing different channels or budget levels.
  • When preparing clear marketing figures for an investor or management.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
TAMTotal Addressable MarketThe full size of the market if everyone who needs the product bought it.
SAMServiceable Addressable MarketThe part of the market you can actually reach with your product and location.
SOMServiceable Obtainable Market (Target Share)The realistic share you expect to win; the tool compares it with your expected annual revenue.
CACCustomer Acquisition CostHow much marketing spend it takes to bring in one new customer.
LTVLifetime ValueThe profit a customer brings over the loyalty period (after meal cost).
ROASReturn on Ad SpendRevenue earned for each unit spent on marketing (e.g. 3x).
4PMarketing Mix (Product, Price, Place, Promotion)The four levers shown in the «Marketing Strategy» section.
Marketing contributionAnnual Marketing ContributionAnnual gross profit (revenue minus meal costs) minus annual marketing costs, before fixed operating expenses.
Competition indexCompetition IndexAverage competitor strength minus average weakness; higher means tougher competition.
Market attractivenessMarket Attractiveness ScoreA 0–10 score combining growth, market size and competition.
Break-even customersBreak-even Customers (Monthly)Monthly customers needed to cover annual marketing costs.
Walk-in customersWalk-in CustomersCustomers who arrive without a paid channel (passers-by, referrals).

Before you start

Gather: market size estimates (TAM, SAM, SOM) as annual values in your currency, the annual growth rate, your main competitors with a 1–10 rating of their strength and weakness, the meal/product price and cost, the list of marketing channels with each one's monthly budget and expected monthly customers, and purchase frequency and loyalty duration.

Choose the currency in «Currency:» and type the beneficiary in «Company Name:»; it appears in the report header and all exported files.

Filling in the data step by step

Project Definition

FieldWhat to enterExample
Project / Product NameThe project name as it should appear in the report and file name.Burger Restaurant
Brief DescriptionOne or two lines describing the idea; shown in the results header.Fast food restaurant specialized in burgers
LocationCity or district.Riyadh
Study Duration (months)Length of the study; shown in the report only, not used in calculations.12

Market Analysis

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total Addressable Market (TAM)Annual value of the whole market in the selected currency; used in the attractiveness score.10000000
Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM)Annual value of the part you can serve; shown in the report.4000000
Target Share (SOM)Realistic annual revenue you target, in currency; compared with calculated revenue.200000
Annual Growth %Annual market growth; type 5 for 5% (the tool divides by 100).5
Key TrendsFree text on market trends; not used in calculations.Healthy options, fast delivery

Target Audience

FieldWhat to enterExample
Age GroupTarget age range as text.18-35
GenderChoose All, Male or Female; descriptive only.All
GeographyGeographic area of the audience.City Center
Income LevelChoose Low, Medium or High; descriptive only.Medium
Interests / BehaviorAudience interests and buying behavior.Burger lovers, prefer delivery
Potential Audience SizeNumber of potential people; shown in the Excel report only.500000

Competitors

The section starts with two empty rows; «Add Competitor» adds a row and × removes it. Rows with an empty name are ignored.

FieldWhat to enterExample
Competitor nameName of the competitor.Burger King
Strength (1-10)Your rating of the competitor's strength, 1 (weak) to 10 (very strong).8
Weakness (1-10)Your rating of its weaknesses, 1 (few) to 10 (many).4

Marketing Strategy

FieldWhat to enterExample
ProductProduct description and advantages; descriptive text.Premium burgers, healthy options
Meal PriceAverage value of one order in currency; the basis of revenue.50
Cost per MealDirect cost of one order in currency; used in LTV.15
Place (Distribution)How the product reaches customers; descriptive text.Strategic location, delivery apps
PromotionPlanned promotion methods; descriptive text.Ads, launch offers
Marketing Team SizeNumber of marketing staff; shown in the report only.2
Plan Duration (months)Months the marketing budget is spent; multiplies the monthly budget.12

Monthly Operating Expenses

FieldWhat to enterExample
RentMonthly rent in currency.20000
SalariesTotal monthly salaries.30000
UtilitiesMonthly electricity, water and internet.5000
OtherAny other monthly operating cost.5000

Note: monthly operating expenses are used in break-even customers and annual operating profit; they are not deducted from the marketing contribution.

Marketing Channels

The section starts with two empty rows; «Add Channel» adds a row, and a channel without a name is ignored.

FieldWhat to enterExample
Channel nameName of the channel.Instagram ads
Monthly budgetMonthly spend on the channel in currency.3000
Expected customers/monthNew customers expected from the channel each month.150

Customer Behavior

FieldWhat to enterExample
Purchases per MonthAverage purchases per customer per month (decimals allowed).2
Loyalty Duration (months)How many months a customer keeps buying on average.6
Walk-in Customers (monthly)Monthly customers who come without a paid channel.1000

When done, click «Calculate Study Now».

How the results are calculated

Results are calculated on the server with these formulas:

  • Monthly active customers = sum of expected channel customers + walk-in customers.
  • Annual revenue = active customers × meal price × purchases per month × 12 (always 12 months).
  • Annual marketing costs = sum of channel monthly budgets × 12; the full plan cost = monthly budget × plan duration (months) is shown separately.
  • Annual gross profit = (meal price − cost per meal) × monthly orders × 12.
  • Marketing contribution = annual gross profit − annual marketing costs.
  • Annual operating profit = marketing contribution − (rent + salaries + utilities + other expenses) × 12.
  • CAC = total monthly budget ÷ total monthly channel customers; 0 if there are no channel customers.
  • ROAS = monthly revenue ÷ monthly marketing budget (2 decimals; equal to the annual-to-annual ratio); 0 if costs are zero.
  • LTV = (meal price − cost per meal) × purchases per month × loyalty duration.
  • Break-even customers = ⌈(monthly marketing budget + monthly fixed costs) ÷ ((meal price − cost per meal) × purchases per month)⌉; ∞ if the meal margin is zero or negative.
  • Consistency check: a warning appears if SOM ≤ SAM ≤ TAM does not hold.
  • Competition index = average strength − average weakness of named competitors.
  • Market attractiveness = [(growth ÷ 100 × 40) + (log10(TAM + 1) × 10) + (max(0, 10 − competition index) × 3)] ÷ 10; then capped at 5 if the marketing contribution is negative, capped at 3 if annual revenue exceeds 1.2 × SOM, and limited to 0–10.

How to read the results

Indicator cards

Nine cards: Active Customers (Monthly), Annual Revenue, Annual Marketing Costs, Annual Marketing Contribution (green when zero or positive, red when negative), Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), Lifetime Value (LTV), Return on Ad Spend (ROAS), Break-even Customers (Monthly) and Annual Operating Profit.

Warnings

  • Meal cost is greater than or equal to the selling price.
  • LTV/CAC ratio is below 3 (ideal above 3), when CAC is above zero.
  • Customer gap: break-even customers exceed active customers, with the number of extra monthly customers needed.
  • Annual revenue exceeds SOM (not realistic), or is below 50% of SOM (the percentage is shown).

Competitor analysis and attractiveness score

IndicatorRangeRating
Competition indexAbove 3Tough market (strong competition)
Competition indexAbove 1 up to 3Moderate competition
Competition index1 or belowExcellent opportunity (weak competition)
Market attractiveness7 or moreGreen (attractive)
Market attractiveness4 to below 7Yellow (average)
Market attractivenessBelow 4Red (weak)

Strategic guidance

  • Positive contribution and ROAS above 2: the model looks promising; consider increasing the budget.
  • Positive contribution and ROAS of 2 or less: review channel efficiency.
  • Zero or negative contribution: marketing spend does not cover its costs; revisit acquisition or pricing.

Charts

The first compares annual revenue with annual marketing costs; the second compares current customers with break-even customers.

Export

The export buttons appear above the results after calculation:

  • «Full Word Export» (blue button): cover (entity, date, currency), basic inputs, indicator cards, warnings, strategic guidance and both charts.
  • PDF button: a formatted image of the whole results section with a header showing the project and entity.
  • «Full Excel Export» (green button): a workbook with 5 sheets — Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Marketing KPIs, Charts, Evaluation & Recommendations — plus a sixth «Warnings» sheet when warnings exist.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Give every competitor and channel a name; rows without a name are ignored.
  • «Add Competitor» and «Add Channel» add a new row and keep what you typed in the existing rows.
  • Enter SOM as annual revenue in the same currency, because the tool compares it directly with annual revenue.
  • All annual indicators use 12 months; «Plan Duration» only sets the full marketing plan cost.
  • Marketing contribution deducts meal and marketing costs; operating profit also deducts rent, salaries and utilities. For full profitability with taxes and investment, use the financial feasibility tool.
  • Aim for LTV/CAC above 3 and ROAS above 2.

More help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; use the side calculator (the «Calculator» button) to work out a number and insert the result into the selected field; and ask the smart assistant (the robot button) to walk you through this tool step by step.

name: Real Estate Investment Return Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool evaluates a rental property investment (apartment, building, shops), bought with cash or with a mortgage, and answers: does the property earn more than the return I require, and when do I get my money back?

It builds the investor's annual cash flows from rent, expenses, property tax and loan payments, adds the property's sale value at the end, then calculates NPV, IRR, MIRR, payback, PI, Cash on Cash and ROI, and gives the project a score out of 100 with a chart and a quick sensitivity analysis.

  • Before buying a property to rent out.
  • To compare an all-cash purchase with a financed one.
  • To test how changes in rent or occupancy affect the return.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
NPVNet Present ValueFuture cash flows discounted to today minus what you paid; positive means profit above your required return.
IRRInternal Rate of ReturnThe actual annual return of the investment; compared with the discount rate.
MIRRModified Internal Rate of ReturnLike IRR, but assumes positive cash flows are reinvested at the reinvestment rate you set.
PIProfitability IndexPresent value of future cash flows ÷ your equity; above 1 means profitable.
ROIReturn on InvestmentTotal net profit over the whole period as a percentage of your equity.
Cash on CashCash-on-Cash ReturnFirst-year cash flow as a percentage of the equity you paid.
LTVLoan-to-ValueShare of the total property cost financed by the bank; 0 means all cash.
NOINet Operating IncomeRent collected minus expenses and property tax, before loan payments.
Discount rateDiscount RateThe minimum annual return you accept; used to bring future money to today's value.
Terminal valueTerminal ValueEstimated sale value of the property at the end of the period.
Debt serviceDebt ServiceTotal annual loan payments (principal + interest).
Assessed valueAssessed ValueMarket value after the assessment discount; property tax is charged on it.
Payback periodPayback PeriodYears until cumulative cash flow becomes positive.

Before you start

Have ready: the purchase price, one-time purchase fees and taxes, number of units and expected monthly rent per unit, monthly expenses, expected occupancy, property tax rate, your expectations for annual rent increase and property appreciation, loan terms if any (share, interest, term), and the minimum return you accept.

Choose the currency in «Currency:» and type the beneficiary in «Entity Name:»; it appears in the report and the exported file name.

Filling in the data step by step

All rates are typed as percentages (5 means 5%) except the numeric occupancy box, which takes a fraction from 0 to 1.

Property & Operations Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Property Value (Initial Cost)Purchase price excluding fees (fees go in their own field). Used for the loan, tax and terminal value.5000000
Number of UnitsNumber of rental units; minimum 1.1
Monthly Rent per UnitAverage monthly rent per unit in currency.25000
Monthly Expenses (Utilities + Maintenance)Monthly operating expenses for the whole property.3000
Occupancy RateThe slider runs 0–100%; the number box next to it takes a fraction 0–1 (0.9 = 90%); both stay in sync.0.9
Annual Property Tax Rate (%)Annual tax rate applied to the assessed value.3.5
Assessed Value Discount (%)Discount applied to market value to get the taxable value.10
Annual Rent Increase (%)Expected yearly rent increase (applies from year 2).5
Annual Land Appreciation (%)Expected yearly increase in property value; sets the sale value at the end.5
Purchase Fees & Taxes (One-time)Registration fees, taxes and commissions paid at purchase.250000

Mortgage Financing (Optional)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Loan-to-Value (LTV) %Loan as a share of total cost (value + fees); 0 means all cash.60
Annual Interest Rate (%)Annual loan interest; 0 is accepted.5
Loan Term (Years)Repayment period from 1 to 30 years.20

Evaluation Criteria

FieldWhat to enterExample
Discount Rate (%)Minimum required annual return; used in NPV, PI and as the finance rate in MIRR.8
Reinvestment Rate (%)Return earned when reinvesting positive cash flows; used in MIRR only.6
Number of YearsHolding period until sale, from 1 to 61 years.20

Then click «Calculate Return».

How the results are calculated

Results are calculated on the server as follows:

  • Total cost = property value + purchase fees; loan = total cost × LTV; equity = total cost − loan.
  • Monthly payment (amortizing loan): P = loan × i × (1+i)^n ÷ ((1+i)^n − 1), i = monthly rate, n = months; with zero interest P = loan ÷ n. Annual debt service = P × 12.
  • Assessed value = property value × (1 − assessment discount).
  • Base annual rent = rent per unit × units × 12 × occupancy.
  • Annual expenses = monthly expenses × 12 + assessed value × tax rate (constant every year).
  • Year 0 = − equity. Year t = base rent × (1 + rent increase)^(t−1) − annual expenses − debt service.
  • The last year also receives the terminal value property value × (1 + appreciation)^years, minus the remaining loan balance if the period is shorter than the loan term.
  • NPV = Σ CF_t ÷ (1 + discount rate)^t; IRR is the rate that makes NPV zero (bisection between −99% and 1000%); «—» is shown if the cash flows never change sign, because no real IRR exists. With 100% financing (zero equity), PI, Cash on Cash and ROI show «∞» instead of dividing by zero.
  • MIRR: future value of positive flows at the reinvestment rate versus present value of negative flows at the discount rate.
  • Payback = (year in which cumulative turns positive − 1) + the fraction of that year; it includes the sale value.
  • PI = PV of years 1..n ÷ equity; Cash on Cash = year-1 cash flow ÷ equity × 100; ROI = sum of all cash flows (incl. year 0) ÷ equity × 100.

How to read the results

Indicator cards

  • Net Present Value (NPV): «Profitable» if positive, «Losing» if negative, «Neutral» at zero.
  • Internal Rate of Return (IRR): shown against the discount rate (> / < / =).
  • Modified IRR (MIRR) with the reinvestment rate used.
  • Payback Period in years, or «None» if the money is not recovered within the period.
  • Profitability Index (PI): «Profitable» above 1, «Not Profitable» below 1, «Neutral» at 1.
  • Cash on Cash Return for year 1 and total Return on Investment (ROI).
  • Leverage (LTV) card with the loan amount, shown only when financing is used.

Project Evaluation (out of 100)

ConditionPoints
NPV above zero30
IRR above the discount rate30
PI above 120
Payback shorter than half the number of years20
ScoreRating
80 or moreExcellent
50 to 79Moderate
Below 50High Risk

Chart and tables

The chart shows annual cash flow (right axis) and cumulative cash flow (left axis). «All Annual Cash Flows» lists the investor cash flow and cumulative total per year, starting with the «Investment» row; negative numbers are red. «When Do We Break Even?» gives the payback year and the final cumulative cash flow.

Sensitivity analysis

«+10% Rent» and «-10% Rent» multiply the rent field by 1.1 or 0.9; «+10% Occupancy» and «-10% Occupancy» add or subtract 0.10 from occupancy (kept between 0 and 1); results recalculate immediately. Changes accumulate with each click, and «↺ Reset» restores the values saved at the last «Calculate Return». The sensitivity table shows NPV, IRR and PI for the current case.

Export

The buttons appear below the sensitivity table:

  • «Full Word Export» (blue button): basic inputs and financing details if any, indicator cards, project evaluation, chart, cash flow table, sensitivity table and payback summary.
  • «Full Excel Export» (green button): a 7-sheet workbook — Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, KPIs, Cash Flows, Sensitivity Analysis, Charts, Evaluation & Recommendations.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Do not include fees in «Property Value» and then enter them again in «Purchase Fees & Taxes», or they will be counted twice.
  • The numeric occupancy box is a fraction (0.95); a number above 1 such as 95 is read as a percentage and converted to 0.95. Zero means no occupancy.
  • The default rent increase (30%) and reinvestment rate (43%) are very high; replace them with realistic figures for your market.
  • Avoid a 100% loan: equity becomes zero and PI and ROI cannot be calculated.
  • Payback includes the sale value at the end, so the money may only be recovered when you sell.
  • Click «Calculate Return» after any manual change so it is saved as the baseline for «Reset».

More help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; use the side calculator (the «Calculator» button) to work out a number and insert the result into the selected field; and ask the smart assistant (the robot button) to walk you through this tool step by step.

name: Advanced Risk Simulation (Monte Carlo)
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool measures the risk of an investment project: it first calculates the «Base Case» (NPV, IRR, payback and PI) from your data, then tests what happens when revenue and costs change, using one of two methods chosen with the buttons at the top:

  • Sensitivity (Two-Way): a 3×3 matrix showing NPV when revenue and costs rise or fall by a percentage you set.
  • Monte Carlo Simulation: thousands of random scenarios to estimate the probability of loss and the expected NPV distribution.

Use it after a financial feasibility study, before presenting a project to a financier, or whenever you need to know how well the project withstands market swings.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
NPVNet Present ValueSum of discounted cash flows minus the initial investment; positive means profitable.
IRRInternal Rate of ReturnThe rate that makes NPV zero; compared with the discount rate.
PIProfitability IndexSum of discounted cash flows ÷ initial investment; above 1 is accepted.
WACCWeighted Average Cost of CapitalThe required return on the project's funds, entered as the discount rate.
EBITEarnings Before Interest and TaxesRevenue − costs − depreciation.
FCFFree Cash FlowAfter-tax profit plus depreciation.
VaR 95%Value at RiskMaximum expected loss at 95% confidence: minus the 5th-percentile NPV, or zero if that percentile is positive.
σSigma / Standard DeviationHow much revenue or costs fluctuate around their expected value.
CVCoefficient of VariationStandard deviation ÷ |mean NPV| × 100; measures relative dispersion.
SkewnessSkewnessDirection of the NPV distribution: positive toward large gains, negative toward losses.
MedianMedianThe NPV with half of the scenarios above it.
Base CaseBase CaseResults with your inputs unchanged.

Before you start

Have ready: the initial investment, expected first-year revenue and operating costs, annual depreciation, expected growth rates, tax rate, required return (WACC) and project duration. You can take them from the financial feasibility tool results.

Choose the currency in «Currency:» and type the beneficiary in «Entity Name:»; it appears in exported reports.

Filling in the data step by step

First choose the analysis type with «Sensitivity (Two-Way)» or «Monte Carlo Simulation»; only that type's fields are shown. Rates are typed as percentages (10 means 10%).

Base Case

FieldWhat to enterExample
Initial InvestmentInitial project cost in currency; must be above zero.545200
Annual Revenue (Year 1)Expected revenue in year 1; must be above zero.2640000
Annual Costs (Year 1)Operating costs in year 1, excluding depreciation.2200000
Annual DepreciationFixed annual depreciation in currency.18750
Annual Revenue Growth (%)Revenue growth rate per year.10
Annual Cost Growth (%)Cost growth rate per year.5
Discount Rate (%)Required return (WACC).10
Tax Rate (%)Income tax rate on positive profit.25
Number of YearsProject duration from 1 to 30 years.8

Sensitivity Variables (Sensitivity mode)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Revenue Change (%)The rise and fall tested on revenue.10
Cost Change (%)The rise and fall tested on costs.10

Monte Carlo Simulation Parameters (Monte Carlo mode)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Revenue Volatility (σ%)Standard deviation of revenue in percent; 0 or empty is replaced by 15.15
Cost Volatility (σ%)Standard deviation of costs in percent; 0 or empty is replaced by 10.10
Number of IterationsNumber of random scenarios; 1000–20000 recommended.5000

Then click «Run Analysis».

How the results are calculated

Calculations run on the server:

  • Revenue in year t = year-1 revenue × (1 + revenue growth)^(t−1); costs likewise with cost growth.
  • EBIT = revenue − costs − depreciation; tax = EBIT × tax rate only when EBIT is positive.
  • FCF = EBIT − tax + depreciation.
  • NPV = − investment + Σ FCF_t ÷ (1 + discount rate)^t; IRR by bisection.
  • Payback = first whole year in which cumulative cash flow ≥ 0 (integer); otherwise «> number of years».
  • PI = sum of discounted cash flows ÷ initial investment.
  • Sensitivity: matrix rows are revenue × (1 − r, 1, 1 + r) and columns costs × (1 − c, 1, 1 + c); each cell is a full NPV.
  • Monte Carlo: each iteration uses revenue = max(0, year-1 revenue × (1 + Z × σ)) and likewise costs, where Z is a random normal number, then computes NPV. VaR 95% = max(0, −5th percentile of NPV), i.e. the loss at the 5th percentile (zero if that percentile is a profit), and P5 NPV is shown with its sign; «Best 5%» the 95th percentile, and probability of loss = share of scenarios with NPV < 0.

How to read the results

Base case cards

  • Base NPV: «Profitable» if above zero, otherwise «Not Profitable».
  • Base IRR: «Above WACC» if it exceeds the discount rate, otherwise a warning.
  • Payback Period in years, marked «Within period» when reached within the project life.
  • Profitability Index (PI): «Accepted» if above 1, otherwise «Rejected».

Sensitivity analysis

The «Two-Way Sensitivity Matrix (NPV)» shows 9 values; the centre cell is the base case and negative values mean a loss. The text below summarises the best scenario (higher revenue, lower costs), the worst scenario, and IRR versus WACC.

Monte Carlo

IndicatorReading
Mean NPV and Median NPVThe average expectation, and the value with 50% of scenarios above it.
VaR 95%Expected maximum loss in 95% of cases (zero means 95% of scenarios are profitable), shown next to the signed P5 NPV.
Best 5%Expected maximum profit (95th percentile).
Probability of LossBelow 20%: Low; 20% to under 50%: Medium; 50% or more: High.
Standard DeviationMeasure of dispersion around the mean.
Coefficient of Variation (CV)Below 50%: Reasonable; 50% or more: High.
SkewnessAbove zero: Positive skew; otherwise: Negative skew.

The «NPV Probability Distribution» chart groups results into 30 bins; red bars are losing scenarios. Simulation results are random and change slightly with each run.

Report verdict: «Project is economically viable» when NPV > 0, IRR > discount rate and PI > 1 all hold; otherwise «Project needs review».

Export

The buttons appear after running the analysis:

  • «Full Excel Export» (green button): a 7-sheet workbook — Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Cash Flows, then Sensitivity Analysis or Monte Carlo depending on the mode, Charts, Evaluation & Recommendations.
  • «Full Word Export» (blue button): cover, inputs, indicators, annual cash flows, the sensitivity matrix or Monte Carlo statistics, and recommendations.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Start with sensitivity to see which variable is more dangerous, then use Monte Carlo to estimate the probability of loss.
  • Base σ on real data or your sector's volatility; only an empty field takes the default; 0 means no volatility.
  • More iterations give steadier results but run slower; 5000 is usually enough.
  • If the probability of loss exceeds 50%, revisit prices or costs before going ahead.
  • Costs exclude depreciation; enter depreciation only in its own field so it is not counted twice.

name: Break-even Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates the break-even point: how many units you must sell each month, and the matching revenue, for sales to cover all fixed and variable costs with no profit and no loss. Every unit sold above that quantity earns a profit.

  • Before launching a product or service, to know the minimum sales needed.
  • When changing price or cost, to see the effect on the sales target.
  • To present a clear sales target to partners or financiers.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
BEPBreak-even PointThe quantity or revenue at which revenue equals total costs.
Fixed costsFixed CostsCosts that do not change with sales volume: rent, salaries, utilities.
Variable costVariable CostDirect material or labour cost per unit; rises with every unit produced.
CMContribution MarginSelling price − variable cost per unit; what each unit contributes toward fixed costs.
CM%Contribution Margin RatioContribution margin ÷ selling price × 100.
Total costsTotal CostsFixed costs + quantity × variable cost.

Before you start

Have ready: total monthly fixed costs, the unit selling price and the variable cost per unit. If you sell several products, use the average price and average variable cost.

Choose the currency in «Currency:» and type the beneficiary in «Entity Name:»; it appears in exported reports.

Filling in the data step by step

FieldWhat to enterExample
Monthly Fixed CostsTotal fixed costs per month (rent, salaries, utilities...) in currency; must be above zero.200000
Unit Selling PriceSelling price of one unit of product or service in currency; must be above zero.120
Variable Cost per UnitDirect material or labour cost per unit in currency; cannot be negative.60

Then click «Calculate Break-even».

How the results are calculated

Results are calculated on the server:

  • Contribution margin = selling price − variable cost.
  • Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin.
  • Break-even revenue = break-even units × selling price.
  • Contribution margin ratio = contribution margin ÷ selling price × 100.
  • If the contribution margin is zero or negative (cost ≥ price) there is no break-even point; «∞» and «Unattainable» are shown.
  • Chart: revenue line = quantity × price; total cost line = fixed costs + quantity × variable cost, from zero to twice the break-even quantity.

How to read the results

  • Break-even Units: units to sell per month (always rounded up to a whole number, since you cannot sell part of a unit).
  • Break-even Revenue: monthly sales needed to cover costs.
  • Contribution Margin per unit and Contribution Margin Ratio.

The «Break-even Chart» shows revenue (green) and total costs (red); the dashed gold line is break-even revenue. Where the lines cross is the break-even point: beyond it is the profit zone, before it the loss zone. The «Analysis Summary» table collects inputs and results.

ConditionVerdict
Contribution margin above zeroPositive contribution margin — break-even achievable
Contribution margin zero or negativeContribution margin is zero or negative — break-even unattainable

Export

The buttons appear after calculation:

  • «Full Word Export» (blue button): inputs, break-even indicators and verdict, chart and summary table.
  • «Full Excel Export» (green button): a 6-sheet workbook — Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, KPIs, Summary, Chart, Interpretation & Recommendations.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Treat break-even units as a minimum and always round up when setting a sales target.
  • Do not put fixed items such as rent into variable cost, or the other way round.
  • Try a slightly higher price or a lower variable cost to see how much the break-even quantity drops.
  • If «Unattainable» appears, the price does not even cover unit cost; review pricing first.

More help

name: Advanced Cash Flow Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates a business's cash flow for one period (month, quarter or year): Operating Cash Flow (OCF) or Free Cash Flow (FCFF), with a full calculation breakdown, then forecasts the next five periods at a growth rate you set.

  • To see whether the business generates real cash after taxes and investment.
  • To estimate monthly or quarterly liquidity from an annual budget.
  • As an input to company valuation or a feasibility study.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
OCFOperating Cash FlowCash generated by operations: net operating profit after tax + depreciation.
FCFFFree Cash Flow to FirmOperating cash flow minus capital expenditures and the change in working capital.
EBITEarnings Before Interest and TaxesRevenue − operating expenses − depreciation.
NOPATNet Operating Profit After TaxEBIT minus tax.
CAPEXCapital ExpendituresAmounts invested in fixed assets (equipment, buildings, systems).
ΔWCChange in Working CapitalIncrease in inventory and receivables minus increase in payables; positive means cash used.
D&ADepreciation & AmortizationA non-cash expense deducted before tax and then added back.

Before you start

Have ready from your budget or financial statements: annual revenue, annual cash operating expenses, annual depreciation, tax rate, annual capital expenditures, the annual change in working capital and the expected growth rate. Always enter annual amounts; the tool divides them automatically for the chosen period.

Choose the currency in «Currency:» and type the beneficiary in «Entity Name:»; it appears in exported reports.

Filling in the data step by step

Settings

FieldWhat to enterExample
Period:Monthly (annual amounts ÷ 12), Quarterly (÷ 4) or Yearly (no division).Yearly
Flow Type:Operating Cash Flow (OCF), or Free Cash Flow (FCFF), which also deducts CAPEX and working capital.Free Cash Flow (FCFF)

Income Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
RevenueTotal annual revenue in currency; must be above zero.1000000
Operating Expenses (excl. depreciation)Annual cash operating expenses, without depreciation.500000
Depreciation & AmortizationAnnual depreciation of fixed assets.50000
Tax Rate (%)Income tax rate on profits, as a percentage (20 means 20%).20
Capital Expenditures (CAPEX)Annual investment in fixed assets; divided per period (affects FCFF only).100000
Change in Working CapitalAnnual change; positive = cash used, negative = cash released (affects FCFF only).20000
Growth Rate per Period (%)Expected cash flow growth for each future period, from −10 to 30.5

Then click «Calculate Cash Flow».

How the results are calculated

Results are calculated on the server (amounts are first divided by 12 or 4 according to the period):

  • EBIT = revenue − operating expenses − depreciation.
  • Tax = EBIT × tax rate only when EBIT is positive, otherwise zero.
  • NOPAT = EBIT − tax.
  • OCF = NOPAT + depreciation.
  • FCFF = OCF − CAPEX − change in working capital.
  • Forecast: flow in period k = current flow × (1 + growth rate)^k for five periods (k = 1..5); so the first forecast period is the one after the current period (next year, quarter or month from today).

How to read the results

  • Cards: revenue for the period, EBIT, NOPAT and the final flow (OCF or FCFF as selected).
  • Final flow status: above zero «Positive», below zero «Negative», zero «Neutral».
  • The «Calculation Breakdown» table shows every step from revenue to the final flow.
  • The «Cash Flow Forecast for Next 5 Periods» table and chart: green bars are positive, red bars negative.
  • The «Interpretation» section describes the current flow and its expected value after five periods.

Note: growth is applied to the flow itself, so a negative flow with a positive growth rate becomes more negative in the forecast.

ConditionReport verdict
Flow above zeroCash flow is positive — healthy liquidity
Flow zero or negativeCash flow is negative or zero — needs review

Export

The buttons appear after calculation:

  • «Full Word Export» (blue button): inputs, indicators with verdict, chart, calculation breakdown, forecast and interpretation.
  • «Full Excel Export» (green button): a 7-sheet workbook — Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Calculation Breakdown, Cash Flow Forecast, Charts, Interpretation & Recommendations.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Enter all amounts as annual figures even when choosing «Monthly» or «Quarterly»; the tool divides them itself.
  • Do not include depreciation in operating expenses, or it will be deducted twice.
  • If OCF is positive but FCFF negative, the cause is usually heavy capital spending or growing inventory and receivables.
  • Use a negative growth rate to test a downturn scenario.

More help

name: Advanced Depreciation Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates the annual depreciation of fixed assets (equipment, vehicles, devices, furniture, etc.) and shows how their book value declines year by year. It answers: how much of the asset cost should be expensed each year, and what is the book value at the end of each year?

Use it when buying a new asset, preparing budgets and financial statements, or comparing depreciation methods before adopting an accounting policy, taking the purchase month into account for a partial first year.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
DepreciationDepreciationSpreading the asset cost over its years of use as an annual expense.
Book ValueBook ValueAsset cost minus accumulated depreciation to date.
Salvage ValueSalvage (Residual) ValueAmount expected to be recovered when the asset is disposed of at the end of its life.
Useful LifeUseful LifeNumber of years the asset is expected to be used.
Accumulated DepreciationAccumulated DepreciationTotal depreciation recorded from purchase to the end of the year.
Straight LineStraight-Line MethodEqual annual charge = (Cost − Salvage) ÷ Life.
Declining BalanceDeclining Balance (1/Life)A fixed rate (1 ÷ Life) applied to the remaining book value, so the charge falls each year.
Double DecliningDouble Declining Balance (2/Life)Like declining balance but with a doubled rate (2 ÷ Life), so early charges are much higher.
Custom RateCustom RateAn annual rate you choose, applied to the book value.
Depreciable AmountDepreciable AmountCost − Salvage; the maximum total depreciation.

Before You Start

  • The purchase invoice and set-up costs (total cost).
  • A realistic estimate of the disposal value and of the expected years of use.
  • The purchase month and the method required by your policy or tax authority.
  • Choose "Currency:" and type the "Entity Name:" at the top; both appear in the results and exported reports.

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Asset Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Asset CostTotal purchase amount in the selected currency.100000
Salvage ValueExpected value at the end of life; it must be lower than the cost or an error message appears.10000
Useful Life (years)Whole number from 1 to 30. If left empty, 5 is used.5

Method and Timing

FieldWhat to enterExample
Depreciation MethodStraight Line, Declining Balance (1/Life), Double Declining (2/Life), or Custom Rate.Straight Line
Annual Depreciation Rate (%)Shown only for Custom Rate. Enter as a percentage (20 means 20%), from 1 to 200. If left empty, 20 is used.20
Purchase MonthThe month the asset was bought; used to compute the partial first year.July

Then click "Calculate Depreciation".

How the Results Are Calculated

  • First-year fraction: Fraction = (12 − (purchase month − 1)) ÷ 12; January = 12/12, July = 6/12, December = 1/12.
  • Straight Line: Annual depreciation = (Cost − Salvage) ÷ Life, multiplied by the fraction in year 1 only.
  • Other methods: Depreciation = Opening book value × Rate, where Rate = 1 ÷ Life (declining), 2 ÷ Life (double), or your rate ÷ 100 (custom); year 1 is multiplied by the fraction.
  • Switch to straight-line (VDB logic): for declining methods the tool also computes Straight-line on remainder = (Book value − Salvage) ÷ Remaining life each year and takes the larger amount; the last year depreciates exactly down to salvage, so book value always ends at salvage. Check example: 100000, salvage 10000, 5 years, January, Double Declining → 40000 / 24000 / 14400 / 8640 / 2960; Declining Balance → 20000 / 17500 / 17500 / 17500 / 17500.
  • Salvage floor: total depreciation never exceeds Cost − Salvage; a year that would exceed it is reduced to the remaining amount, and the schedule stops once salvage is reached.
  • Schedule length: at most Life + 1 years (the extra year absorbs the remainder after a mid-year purchase).
  • Final Book Value = Cost − Total Depreciation; Avg Annual Depreciation = Total Depreciation ÷ Actual Years.

How to Read the Results

  • Cards: "Total Depreciation", "Final Book Value", "Actual Years", "Avg Annual Depreciation" and "Annual Depreciation Rate" (labelled "Fixed" for Straight Line or "Effective" for the other methods).
  • "Book Value Over Time" chart: a line showing the year-end book value; a straight line indicates Straight Line, a curve indicates a declining method.
  • "Annual Depreciation Schedule": for each year: Annual Depreciation, Accumulated Depreciation, Book Value.

This tool has no good/bad rating thresholds. As general guidance, choose the method that reflects how the asset is actually used; assets that lose value quickly (computers, vehicles) suit the declining methods.

Export

  • "Full Excel Export" (green button): a 6-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Depreciation Schedule, Chart, Interpretation & Recommendations.
  • "Full Word Export" (blue button): a report with the basic inputs, performance indicators, the chart image, the annual depreciation schedule and recommendations.

Click "Calculate Depreciation" before exporting.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • Make sure the asset cost is greater than the salvage value, otherwise nothing is calculated.
  • Type the custom rate as a percentage (20, not 0.2).
  • For a mid-year purchase, expect a schedule of Life + 1 years.
  • With declining methods, check the final book value; it may remain above salvage.
  • Use the method and useful life accepted by your local tax rules when preparing tax returns.

Additional Help
