name: Advanced WACC Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC): the average annual cost a company pays for the money it gets from shareholders and lenders combined. It answers: what is the minimum return a project must earn to be worth financing?

Use it as the discount rate in project valuation (NPV), as the hurdle to compare with a project’s expected return (IRR), or to see how changing the debt mix affects financing cost. The cost of equity can be entered manually or computed with the CAPM model.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
WACCWeighted Average Cost of CapitalThe average cost of all funding sources, weighted by the size of each source.
CAPMCapital Asset Pricing ModelA method to estimate the return shareholders require based on the stock’s risk.
EEquityMoney provided by shareholders or owners.
DDebtInterest-bearing loans and bonds.
VValue = E + DTotal financing: equity plus debt.
ReCost of EquityAnnual return shareholders expect for their investment.
RdCost of DebtAnnual interest rate on borrowings, before tax.
RfRisk-Free RateReturn on a near-riskless investment such as government bonds.
β (Beta)Beta coefficientHow much the company’s stock moves relative to the market; 1 = same as the market.
Rm − RfMarket Risk PremiumExtra return investors demand for investing in the market instead of safe assets.
TTax RateIncome tax rate; interest is tax-deductible, so the effective cost of debt falls.
NPV / IRRNet Present Value / Internal Rate of ReturnProject appraisal measures that use WACC as the discount rate or hurdle rate.
WeightWeightEach source’s share of total financing (E/V or D/V).

Before You Start

  • Market value of equity (or paid-in capital for unlisted companies) and the value of interest-bearing debt.
  • Average interest rate on loans and the income tax rate.
  • Either an agreed cost of equity, or CAPM data: government bond yield, Beta and market risk premium.
  • Choose "Currency:" and type the "Entity Name:" at the top; both appear in the results and reports.

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Equity and Its Cost

FieldWhat to enterExample
EquityAmount in the selected currency.1000000
Cost of Equity (Re) Method"Manual Entry" or CAPM; the visible fields change with your choice.Manual Entry
Cost of Equity (Re) (%)Manual Entry only. Percentage: 12 means 12%.12

CAPM Fields (shown when CAPM is selected)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Risk-Free Rate (Rf) (%)Percentage: 3 means 3%.3
Beta (β)A plain number, not a percentage. If left empty, the tool uses 1; 0 is accepted and means an asset with no market risk.1.2
Market Risk Premium (Rm - Rf) (%)Percentage: 5 means 5%. Enter the premium itself, not the full market return.5

Debt and Tax

FieldWhat to enterExample
DebtAmount in the selected currency (can be 0 if there are no loans).500000
Cost of Debt (Rd) (%)Annual pre-tax interest rate as a percentage.5
Tax Rate (%)Income tax rate as a percentage.20

Then click "Calculate WACC". Equity or debt must be greater than zero.

How the Results Are Calculated

  • Cost of equity: as entered (manual), or with CAPM: Re = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf).
  • Weights: V = E + D, Equity weight = E ÷ V, Debt weight = D ÷ V.
  • After-tax cost of debt: Rd × (1 − T).
  • Result: WACC = (E/V × Re) + (D/V × Rd × (1 − T)), shown as a percentage with two decimals.

Example with the defaults: V = 1500000, weights 66.67% and 33.33%, after-tax cost of debt = 5% × 0.8 = 4%, so WACC = 0.6667 × 12% + 0.3333 × 4% = 9.33%.

How to Read the Results

  • WACC card: the rate with its rating, Equity Weight, Debt Weight, Cost of Equity (Re) and After-Tax Cost of Debt.
  • "Capital Structure": a pie chart of equity (green) versus debt (red).
  • "Calculation Breakdown": value, weight and cost of each source, pre-tax and after-tax debt, then WACC.
  • "Interpretation": a sentence explaining what the rate means.

Rating thresholds used by the tool:

WACCRatingMeaning
Below 8%Very LowCheap financing, positive for investment projects.
8% to below 12%Low to ModerateReasonable financing cost.
12% to below 16%Relatively HighCompare it with expected project returns.
16% or moreVery HighIt may be hard to earn returns above this cost.

The rating is shown in green when WACC is below 12% and in a warning colour otherwise. General decision rule: accept a project when its expected return (IRR) exceeds WACC.

Export

  • "Full Excel Export" (green button): a 6-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Calculation Breakdown, Capital Structure Chart, Interpretation & Recommendations.
  • "Full Word Export" (blue button): a report with the basic inputs, performance indicators, the capital structure chart, the calculation breakdown and the interpretation.

Calculate WACC before exporting.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • Enter all rates as percentages (12, not 0.12) and Beta as a plain number (1.2).
  • Use market values where possible, not only book values.
  • In CAPM enter the premium (Rm − Rf), not the full market return, or Re will be overstated.
  • Beta = 0 is accepted (an asset with no market risk, so Re = Rf); leaving the field empty makes the tool use 1.
  • Do not include supplier payables in debt; include only interest-bearing borrowings.

Additional Help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (the "Calculator" button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (the robot button) explains the steps for this tool.

name: Return on Investment (ROI) Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool measures the annual Return on Investment (ROI) and the payback period, and plots cumulative cash flow so you can see when the investment turns from loss to profit. It answers: how much does this investment return each year for every unit spent, and when do I get my money back?

Use it for a quick assessment of a project idea, an equipment purchase or a marketing campaign, or to compare several opportunities assuming a constant profit each year.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
ROIReturn on InvestmentAnnual profit as a percentage of the investment cost; 25% means every 100 returns 25 per year.
Payback PeriodPayback PeriodNumber of years needed to recover the investment cost from profits.
Net ProfitNet ProfitRevenue minus all expenses and taxes.
Cumulative Cash FlowCumulative Cash FlowTotal received to date minus the initial cost; starts negative and then rises.
Year 0Year 0The moment the investment is paid, before any profit.

Before You Start

  • Total investment cost (purchase, fit-out, initial working capital).
  • An estimate of net profit after all expenses, and the period that figure covers (year, half-year, quarter, month).
  • Choose "Currency:" and type the "Entity Name:" at the top; both appear in the results and reports.

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Investment Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total Investment CostAmount greater than zero in the selected currency.100000
Expected Annual Net ProfitNet profit for the period chosen in the next field (despite the word "Annual"). It can be negative if you expect a loss.25000
Profit PeriodYearly, Half-Yearly, Quarterly or Monthly.Yearly
Number of Years to DisplayWhole number from 1 to 20; if empty, 5 is used. Affects the chart only.5

Then click "Calculate ROI".

How the Results Are Calculated

  • Annual profit: Annual profit = Entered profit ÷ Period factor, where the factor is 1 (yearly), 0.5 (half-yearly), 0.25 (quarterly) or 0.0833 (monthly, i.e. about ×12).
  • Return: ROI = (Annual profit ÷ Investment cost) × 100; this is an annual return, not a multi-year total.
  • Payback: Cost ÷ Annual profit in years; if profit is zero or negative, "∞" is shown (no payback).
  • Cumulative cash flow: Year 0 = −Cost, then the annual profit is added each year up to the chosen number of years.

Example with the defaults: 25000 ÷ 100000 = ROI of 25% and a payback of 4 years.

How to Read the Results

  • Cards: "Return on Investment (ROI)" with its status, "Payback Period" in years, "Annual Net Profit" after conversion, and "Investment Cost".
  • Status on the card: ROI above 0: "Profitable"; below 0: "Losing"; exactly 0: "Neutral".
  • "Cumulative Cash Flow Over Time" chart: red points are years where the cumulative total is still negative, green points come after payback; the switch from red to green marks the payback year.

The written interpretation in the exported reports uses these thresholds:

ROIInterpretation
Above 20%Excellent investment with very high return.
Above 10% up to 20%Good investment with reasonable return.
Above 0% up to 10%Acceptable investment but return is relatively low.
0% or lessLoss-making investment, recommended to re-evaluate.

The recommendations paragraph in the Excel file uses the same limits (20% / 10% / 0%) as the screen. In the KPI sheet the payback period is coloured green when it is under 5 years.

Export

  • "Full Excel Export" (green button): a 5-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Chart, Interpretation & Recommendations.
  • "Full Word Export" (blue button): a report with the basic inputs, performance indicators, the cumulative cash flow chart and the interpretation.

Calculate ROI before exporting.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • Pick the correct period: monthly profit entered with "Yearly" gives an ROI about 12 times too low.
  • Use net profit after all expenses and taxes, not revenue.
  • The tool assumes the same profit every year and ignores the time value of money; for long projects use the NPV/IRR analysis tool.
  • "Number of Years to Display" changes neither ROI nor payback.
  • Include initial working capital in the cost so the return is not overstated.

Additional Help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (the "Calculator" button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (the robot button) explains the steps for this tool.

name: Advanced Loan Amortization Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool builds a full repayment schedule for any equal-instalment loan, with an optional down payment, an extra payment with each instalment, and an initial grace period. It answers: what is the periodic payment, how much interest will I pay in total, and how many years do I save by paying a little extra?

Use it before signing a bank loan, equipment or property financing, to compare financing offers, or to plan the cash flow needed for debt service.

Terms and Abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
PrincipalPrincipalThe amount actually borrowed after the down payment.
Periodic PaymentPeriodic Payment (PMT)The fixed amount paid each period, made up of interest and part of the principal.
Amortization ScheduleAmortization ScheduleA table showing, for each payment, the interest, principal repaid and remaining balance.
Annual Interest RateAnnual (Nominal) Interest RateThe yearly rate; divided by payments per year to get the rate per period.
Down PaymentDown PaymentAmount paid upfront that reduces the amount borrowed.
Extra PaymentExtra PaymentAmount added to each instalment that goes entirely to reducing principal.
Grace PeriodGrace PeriodMonths at the start with no instalments, during which interest accrues on the balance.
Interest CapitalizationInterest CapitalizationAdding unpaid interest to the loan balance so that it later earns interest itself.
Remaining BalanceRemaining BalancePrincipal still outstanding after each payment.

Before You Start

  • The loan amount, annual rate, term and payment frequency from the bank offer or contract.
  • Any down payment or extra payment you plan, and the length of the grace period if any.
  • Choose "Currency:" and type the "Entity Name:" at the top; both appear in the results and reports.

Filling In the Data Step by Step

Loan Information

FieldWhat to enterExample
Loan AmountTotal amount before the down payment, greater than zero.100000
Annual Interest Rate (%)Percentage: 5 means 5%. 0% is accepted (interest-free loan); the payment is then amount borrowed ÷ number of payments.5
Loan Term (Years)From 1 to 50; if empty, 10 is used.10
Payment FrequencyMonthly, Quarterly, Semi-Annually or Annually.Monthly

Advanced Settings (Down Payment, Extra Payment, Grace Period)

Click this heading to open the fields:

FieldWhat to enterExample
Down PaymentAmount deducted from the loan amount; 0 if none.20000
Extra PaymentAmount added to every instalment after the grace period; 0 if none.200
Grace Period (Months)Whole number from 0 to 60 months; it is part of the loan term, not added to it.6

Then click "Calculate Amortization Schedule".

How the Results Are Calculated

  • Amount borrowed = Loan amount − Down payment (not below zero).
  • Number of payments n = Years × Frequency; Rate per period r = Annual rate ÷ Frequency.
  • Grace period: converted to periods: g = round(Grace months × Frequency ÷ 12), capped at n − 1. In each grace period nothing is paid and the interest is added to the balance.
  • Instalment: on the post-grace balance B over the remaining m = n − g periods: PMT = B × r × (1 + r)^m ÷ ((1 + r)^m − 1), and at 0% interest PMT = B ÷ m (check: 100000 at 6% for 5 years monthly = 1933.28; 120000 at 0% for 10 years monthly = 1000), then Periodic payment = PMT + Extra payment.
  • Each payment: Interest = Balance × r, Principal repaid = Payment − Interest; the last payment equals what is actually left, and the schedule stops once the balance is cleared.
  • Years saved = Loan term − (Actual payments ÷ Frequency), shown only when there is an extra payment.

How to Read the Results

  • Cards: "Periodic Payment" (marked "Includes extra" when an extra payment is set), "Total Interest" (including interest capitalized during the grace period), "Total Payments", and "Actual Number of Payments" (grace-period rows are counted too) with years saved.
  • "Summary": automatic notes: years saved by the extra payment, principal after the down payment, the grace period, and a warning if total interest exceeds 50% of the principal after the down payment; if none applies, "Indicators look good" is shown.
  • "Total Interest vs Principal Distribution": a pie chart of interest (red) versus borrowed principal (green).
  • "Periodic Payment Distribution": stacked bars for up to the first 60 payments, showing the interest part shrinking and the principal part growing over time.
  • "Full Amortization Schedule": Payment #, Payment, Interest, Principal, Remaining Balance; grace-period rows show a payment of 0 and a rising balance.

Thresholds used by the tool: an on-screen warning when total interest is more than 50% of the principal after the down payment; in the Excel KPI sheet total interest is coloured green when it is below 30% of the loan amount and red otherwise.

Export

  • "Full Excel Export" (green button): a 6-sheet workbook: Cover Page, Inputs & Assumptions, Key Performance Indicators, Amortization Schedule, Charts, Interpretation & Recommendations.
  • "Full Word Export" (blue button): a report with the basic inputs, performance indicators, charts and the repayment schedule.

Calculate the schedule before exporting.

Tips and Common Mistakes

  • A grace period is not free: interest is added to the balance, raising the instalment and total interest.
  • The loan term includes the grace period; a 10-year loan with 12 months of grace is repaid over 9 years.
  • Even a small extra payment with each instalment clearly reduces interest and term; try several amounts.

content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool analyses monthly labor cost against sales and measures staff productivity and distribution across shifts. It answers: are headcount and wages right for the sales volume, or is there wage waste or understaffing?

Use it in restaurants, cafés, shops and service centres when planning a new branch, building a shift roster, or reviewing payroll when costs rise.

name: Financial & Consulting Calculator
content:

The "Consulting Calculator" is a scientific and financial calculator that records every operation in an "Operation Log" you can filter and export. It answers quick everyday questions: what is the price after tax or discount, what is the return on a given cost, and how much simple interest does an amount earn over a period?

name: Multi-Product Break-Even Analysis
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates the break-even point for a business that sells several products with different prices and costs (dishes, drinks, services). It uses the sales mix between products and then allocates break-even units and revenue to each product.

The question it answers: how much do I need to sell each month, in revenue and in units of each product, to cover fixed costs with neither profit nor loss, and how far are my current sales from that point?

Use it when pricing a new menu, changing prices or suppliers, before opening a branch, or during a monthly performance review.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
BEP / Break-evenBreak-Even PointThe sales level at which revenue equals total costs: no profit, no loss.
BE Units / BE RevenueBreak-Even Units / Break-Even RevenueThe number of units or the revenue amount needed to reach break-even.
CMContribution MarginSelling price minus variable cost per unit: what each unit contributes towards fixed costs and then profit.
CM RatioContribution Margin RatioContribution margin divided by selling price: how much of each unit of revenue is left after variable costs.
MOSMargin of SafetyActual revenue minus break-even revenue: how far sales can fall before you start making a loss.
Sales mixSales MixEach product's share of the total number of units sold.
Weighted averageWeighted AverageAn average in which each product is weighted by its share of the mix.
Fixed costsFixed CostsCosts that do not change with sales volume, such as rent, salaries and insurance.
Variable costVariable CostA cost that rises with every unit sold, such as ingredients, packaging and delivery commission.

Before you start

  • The product list with each product's selling price and variable cost per unit (for example from recipe cost cards).
  • Each product's share of units sold (from POS reports for the last month or an average of several months).
  • Total monthly fixed costs and, optionally, total units actually sold in the month.
  • Choose the currency in "Currency:" (USD, EUR, TRY, EGP, KWD, SAR) and type the beneficiary in "Entity Name:", which appears on the report cover and in the file name.

Filling in the data step by step

Products (Dishes / Beverages)

The page starts with three empty rows. Use "Add Product" to add a row and the × button to delete one (the first row cannot be deleted). Any row missing a name, price, cost or mix is ignored in the calculation.

FieldWhat to enterExample
Product nameName of the dish, drink or service.Burger
Selling priceSelling price of one unit in the selected currency, preferably excluding VAT.10
Variable costVariable cost of one unit in the same currency (ingredients, packaging, commissions). It must be lower than the selling price.4
Mix %The product's share of total units sold, as a percentage (50 means 50%). If the shares do not add up to 100 they are rescaled automatically.50

Fixed Costs

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total Monthly Fixed CostsMonthly amount in the selected currency of all costs that do not change with sales (rent, salaries, utilities, insurance).20000

Actual Sales (Optional)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total Actual Units Sold during the monthTotal units actually sold across all products in the month (a count, not an amount). Used only for the margin of safety; leave empty if unavailable.4000

How the results are calculated

  1. Mix normalisation: product share = its mix ÷ sum of all mixes (a zero sum is treated as 1).
  2. For each product: CM = selling price − variable cost and CM Ratio = CM ÷ selling price.
  3. Weighted average price: Σ (share × price); weighted average CM: Σ (share × CM).
  4. Weighted CM ratio: weighted average CM ÷ weighted average price (zero if the average price is zero).
  5. Total break-even units = fixed costs ÷ weighted average CM.
  6. Break-even revenue = break-even units × weighted average price (mathematically equal to fixed costs ÷ weighted ratio); then product BE units = total × its share and product BE revenue = its units × its price. Units are displayed rounded up to the next whole unit.
  7. Margin of safety (when actual sales are entered): actual revenue = actual units × weighted average price, MOS = actual revenue − break-even revenue, MOS% = MOS ÷ actual revenue × 100.

Example: Burger (10, cost 4, mix 50), Pizza (12, cost 5, mix 30), Juice (4, cost 1, mix 20), fixed costs 20000. Weighted average price 9.40, CM ratio 60.6%, break-even revenue about 32982, break-even units 3509 (1755 burgers, 1053 pizzas, 702 juices). With 4000 actual units the margin of safety is about 4618 (12.3%).

Note: if the weighted average CM is zero or negative, break-even cannot be reached and «∞» is shown with a warning. Warnings also appear for incomplete rows (excluded from the calculation) and for products with a negative margin. The pie chart shows each product’s share of total contribution margin (share × CM).

How to read the results

  • Indicator cards: Weighted Avg Price, CM Ratio, Break-Even Revenue (monthly), Total Break-Even Units.
  • Product table: for each product the price, variable cost, CM and CM ratio, normalised mix %, BE units and BE revenue.
  • Pie chart: each product’s share of total contribution margin (mix share × unit CM).
  • Bar chart: break-even units required for each product.
  • Margin of Safety card: the amount and percentage by which revenue can drop before reaching break-even. A negative value means current sales are below break-even (a loss). Without actual sales it shows "Not determined".

The code does not apply rating thresholds. As general guidance only: the higher the margin of safety, the better the business can absorb a sales drop; a very small margin calls for reviewing prices, costs or the mix.

Export

Export is available after you click "Calculate Break-Even Point".

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the entity name and date, break-even indicators, margin of safety (if available), product breakdown table, a chart image and recommendations.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a workbook with 6 sheets: Report Cover, Inputs & Products, Break-Even Results, Product Detail, Charts and Recommendations (interpretation, improving the mix, margin of safety, disclaimer).

Tips and common mistakes

  • The mix is a share of units, not of sales value; derive it from the number of items sold per product.
  • Do not put fixed salaries or rent in variable cost, nor recipe ingredients in fixed costs.
  • Make sure each product's variable cost is below its selling price; otherwise every sale deepens the loss.
  • Fill in all four fields of every row; an incomplete row is silently excluded.
  • Try shifting the mix towards higher-margin products and watch the break-even point fall.

name: Comprehensive Financial Ratios Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates 19 financial ratios from balance-sheet and income-statement data, grouped into four categories: Liquidity, Profitability, Solvency and Activity. Most ratios are rated Good / Acceptable / Poor, and automatic recommendations are generated.

ROAReturn on AssetsNet profit ÷ total assets: how much the company earns on each unit of assets it owns.
ROEReturn on EquityNet profit ÷ equity: the return on the owners' money.
EBITEarnings Before Interest and TaxesOperating profit; used in the interest coverage ratio.
COGSCost of Goods SoldThe direct cost of the products or services sold.
A/RAccounts ReceivableAmounts customers owe the company.
A/PAccounts PayableAmounts the company owes suppliers.
DIO / Days InventoryDays Inventory OutstandingAverage number of days stock is held before being sold.
DSODays Sales OutstandingAverage number of days to collect cash from customers.
DPO / Days PayablesDays Payables OutstandingAverage number of days the company takes to pay suppliers.
CCCCash Conversion CycleDays between paying for stock and collecting cash from its sale: DIO + DSO − DPO.
LiquidityLiquidityAbility to pay obligations due within a year from current assets.
SolvencySolvencyAbility to carry the company's debt over the long term.
EquityShareholders' equityTotal assets minus total liabilities; the tool calculates it automatically.
Current assets / liabilitiesCurrent Assets / Current LiabilitiesItems that turn into cash or fall due within one year.

Before you start

  • Gather the balance sheet and income statement for one year (annual values), preferably audited.
  • You also need receivable and payable balances and, if any, the value of credit sales.
  • Choose the currency in "Currency:" and type the beneficiary in "Entity Name:", which appears on the report cover and in the file name. Enter all amounts in the same currency.

Filling in the data step by step

All fields are numbers; an empty field counts as zero, except "Credit Sales (Optional)", which equals revenue when left empty.

Balance Sheet (Annual Values)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Cash & EquivalentsCash on hand, current bank accounts and very short-term deposits at the balance-sheet date.100000
InventoryValue of goods, raw materials and work in progress.200000
Other Current AssetsAll other current assets, including the receivables balance, short-term investments and prepaid expenses.100000
Fixed AssetsNet value of buildings, machinery, equipment and other long-term assets.500000
Current LiabilitiesDebts due within one year (suppliers, short-term loans, current instalments).300000
Long-Term LiabilitiesLoans and bonds due after more than one year.200000

Income Statement & Cash Flows

FieldWhat to enterExample
Revenue (Sales)Annual net sales (cash and credit).2000000
Cost of Goods SoldAnnual cost of goods sold (COGS).1200000
Operating ExpensesAnnual selling, administrative and marketing expenses, excluding interest and tax.400000
Interest ExpenseTotal annual interest on loans.50000
Tax Rate (%)Income tax rate as a percentage: 25 means 25%. Default is 25.25
Credit Sales (Optional)Annual sales made on credit. If empty (or zero) it is taken as equal to revenue.800000
Accounts Receivable (A/R)Amount owed by customers at the balance-sheet date; used only for receivables turnover.150000
Accounts Payable (A/P)Amount owed to suppliers at the balance-sheet date; used only for payables turnover.100000

How the results are calculated

Intermediate values

  • Current assets = cash + inventory + other current assets
  • Total assets = current assets + fixed assets, total liabilities = current + long-term
  • Equity = total assets − total liabilities
  • Operating profit (EBIT) = revenue − COGS − operating expenses
  • Profit before tax = EBIT − interest expense; net profit = profit before tax × (1 − tax rate) if positive; a loss is kept as is, with no tax.

Ratios

  • Liquidity: Current Ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities, Quick Ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities, Cash Ratio = cash ÷ current liabilities.
  • Profitability: Gross Profit Margin = (revenue − COGS) ÷ revenue, Operating Profit Margin = EBIT ÷ revenue, Net Profit Margin = net profit ÷ revenue, ROA = net profit ÷ total assets, ROE = net profit ÷ equity.
  • Solvency: Debt to Equity = total liabilities ÷ equity, Debt to Assets = total liabilities ÷ total assets, Interest Coverage = EBIT ÷ interest expense, Equity Ratio = equity ÷ total assets.
  • Activity: Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ inventory, Days Inventory = 365 ÷ inventory turnover, Receivables Turnover = credit sales ÷ receivables, DSO = 365 ÷ receivables turnover, Payables Turnover = COGS ÷ payables, Days Payables = 365 ÷ payables turnover, CCC = Days Inventory + DSO − Days Payables.

Special rules: if a ratio’s denominator is zero, the ratio shows «—» rated «Undefined» instead of a misleading zero. If interest expense is zero, interest coverage shows «N/A (no interest)». With zero or negative equity, ROE and Debt to Equity are not calculated («—») because they are meaningless. Days are computed as 365 × balance ÷ (COGS or credit sales) and equal 0 when there is no balance. A warning appears if receivables exceed «Other Current Assets», since they are part of it.

How to read the results

Cards: Current Ratio, Net Profit Margin, ROA, ROE, Debt to Equity, Cash Conversion Cycle (Days), plus a card with Total Current Assets, Total Assets, Total Liabilities and Equity (tagged "Positive" or "Negative").

Ratios table: Category, Ratio, Value, Assessment. Rating thresholds used in the code:

RatioRating thresholds
Current Ratio1.5 or more: Good; 1 to below 1.5: Acceptable; below 1: Poor
Quick Ratio1 or more: Good; 0.5 to below 1: Acceptable; below 0.5: Poor
Cash Ratio0.5 or more: Good; 0.2 to below 0.5: Acceptable; below 0.2: Poor
Gross Profit Margin40% or more: Good; 20% to below 40%: Acceptable; below 20%: Poor
Operating Profit Margin20% or more: Good; 10% to below 20%: Acceptable; below 10%: Poor
Net Profit Margin15% or more: Good; 5% to below 15%: Acceptable; below 5%: Poor
ROA10% or more: Good; 5% to below 10%: Acceptable; below 5%: Poor
ROE20% or more: Good; 10% to below 20%: Acceptable; below 10%: Poor
Debt to Equity1 or less: Good; above 1 up to 2: Acceptable; above 2: Poor; zero or negative equity: «—» Undefined
Debt to Assets0.5 or less: Good; above 0.5 up to 0.7: Acceptable; above 0.7: Poor
Interest Coverage3 or more: Good; 1.5 to below 3: Acceptable; below 1.5: Poor
Equity Ratio50% or more: Good; 30% to below 50%: Acceptable; below 30%: Poor
Cash Conversion CycleBelow 0: Excellent; 0 to below 60 days: Acceptable; 60 days or more: Long

Turnover ratios are shown in "Times" without a rating, and day counts are shown without a rating.

Recommendations & Analysis: one liquidity message is always shown (current ratio below 1: very low liquidity; 1 to below 1.5: acceptable; 1.5 or more: good), plus extra alerts when the quick ratio is below 0.5, ROE is below 10%, debt to equity is above 2, interest coverage is below 1.5, or the CCC is negative (excellent supplier financing) or above 90 days.

Radar chart (0–100): Liquidity = current ratio × 50, Profitability = net margin × 400, Solvency = (1 − debt to assets) × 100, Activity = (inventory turnover ÷ 10) × 100, each capped at 100. Bar chart: ROA, ROE and net profit margin in percent.

Export

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the entity name, date and currency, the summary cards, the full ratios table, a chart image and the recommendations.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a workbook with 5 sheets: Report Cover, Financial Inputs, Financial Ratios, Charts and Recommendations.

Export works after you click "Calculate Financial Ratios".

Tips and common mistakes

  • Include the receivables balance in "Other Current Assets" as well; the "Accounts Receivable (A/R)" field is used only for DSO and is not added to assets.
  • If the company has no loans, enter interest as 0; interest coverage then shows «N/A (no interest)» with no negative rating.
  • Use full-year figures; monthly figures make the inventory, collection and payment days wrong because the calculation uses 365 days.
  • Type the tax rate as a number like 20, not 0.20.
  • If equity shows "Negative", liabilities exceed assets; check the figures first, then address the debt.

Additional help

name: Advanced Financial Forecasting
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool builds a multi-year financial forecast from base-year revenue, a growth rate and cost ratios. It produces a projected income statement, calculates working capital and free cash flow year by year, and values the project with NPV, IRR, payback period and terminal value.

The question it answers: is this project or business worth the required investment, and what are its future cash flows worth today?

Use it to evaluate an expansion or the purchase of an existing business, to prepare a business plan for an investor or bank, or to test how changes in growth or costs affect value.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
NPVNet Present ValueToday's value of all future cash flows after discounting, minus the initial investment. Positive means the project creates value.
IRRInternal Rate of ReturnThe discount rate at which NPV equals zero: the project's implied annual return.
WACCWeighted Average Cost of CapitalThe average cost of debt and equity financing; used here as the discount rate.
FCFFree Cash FlowCash left after operations, taxes, investment in fixed assets and working capital.
EBITEarnings Before Interest and TaxesRevenue minus COGS, operating expenses and depreciation.
COGSCost of Goods SoldThe direct cost of the products sold.
CAPEXCapital ExpenditureSpending on buying or renewing fixed assets.
DSODays Sales OutstandingAverage days until customers pay.
DIODays Inventory OutstandingAverage days stock is held before being sold.
DPODays Payables OutstandingAverage days until the company pays suppliers.
WCWorking CapitalReceivables + inventory − payables: cash tied up in the operating cycle.
Terminal ValueTerminal ValueThe value of all cash flows after the last forecast year, assuming constant perpetual growth (Gordon model).
DepreciationDepreciationSpreading the cost of fixed assets over their useful life; a non-cash expense.
Payback PeriodPayback PeriodYears until cumulative free cash flow covers the initial investment.

Before you start

  • Revenue for the last full year and COGS and operating expenses as a percentage of revenue (from the financial statements).
  • Annual depreciation, expected annual CAPEX and the initial investment amount.
  • Collection, inventory and payment days, and the current working-capital balance.
  • Your estimates of growth, discount rate (WACC) and perpetual growth.
  • Choose the currency in "Currency:" and type the beneficiary in "Entity Name:", which appears in the report and file name.

Filling in the data step by step

All rates are typed as percentages: 10 means 10% (the tool divides by 100). Amounts are in the selected currency.

Historical Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Base Year RevenueRevenue in the last available year (amount). Forecast year 1 = this value × (1 + growth).2000000
COGS (% of Revenue)Cost of goods sold as a percentage of revenue. Default 60.60
Operating Expenses (% of Revenue)Operating expenses as a percentage of revenue, excluding depreciation. Default 25.25
Tax Rate (%)Income tax rate applied to positive profit. Default 25.25
Annual DepreciationA fixed depreciation amount for every year.50000
Annual CAPEXA fixed amount invested in fixed assets every year.80000
Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)Number of days. Default 45.45
Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO)Number of days. Default 60.60
Days Payables Outstanding (DPO)Number of days. Default 30.30

Growth & Valuation Assumptions

FieldWhat to enterExample
Annual Revenue Growth Rate (%)Constant growth each year. Default 10; a negative number models decline.10
Forecast Period (Years)A whole number of years. Default 5 when empty; 1 to 50.5
Discount Rate (WACC) (%)Required return on the investment. Default 10% when empty; 0 is calculated as zero.12
Initial Working CapitalWorking capital in the base year (amount); subtracted from year-1 working capital to get the change.200000
Initial Investment (Year 0 CAPEX)The amount invested today before cash flows start.500000
Perpetual Growth Rate (%)Growth of cash flows after the last forecast year; must be below the discount rate. Default 3% when empty; 0 means no growth after the forecast.3

How the results are calculated

For each year t from 1 to the number of years:

  • Revenue = base revenue × (1 + growth)^t
  • COGS = revenue × COGS %, operating expenses = revenue × OpEx %
  • EBIT = revenue − COGS − operating expenses − depreciation
  • Tax = EBIT × tax rate if EBIT is positive, otherwise zero; net income = EBIT − tax (the model has no interest).
  • Working capital = (DSO ÷ 365 × revenue) + (DIO ÷ 365 × COGS) − (DPO ÷ 365 × COGS)
  • Change in WC = this year's WC − last year's WC (year 1: − initial working capital).
  • FCF = net income + depreciation − CAPEX − change in WC

Valuation:

  • Terminal value = last-year FCF × (1 + perpetual growth) ÷ (discount rate − perpetual growth); zero if the discount rate does not exceed perpetual growth.
  • NPV = −initial investment + Σ FCF ÷ (1 + discount rate)^t + terminal value ÷ (1 + discount rate)^years
  • IRR: the rate that makes the present value of the flows (−initial investment, yearly FCF, with terminal value added to the last year) equal zero. It shows "N/A" if the flows do not include both positive and negative values. The IRR of the forecast period only (without terminal value) is shown next to it for comparison; 0% is shown as is.
  • Payback: the year in which cumulative FCF (undiscounted, without terminal value) reaches the initial investment, plus a proportional fraction within that year. If not reached within the forecast, "Not achieved" or ∞ is shown. With zero initial investment, payback is 0.

Example with the defaults plus revenue 2000000, depreciation 50000, CAPEX 80000, initial working capital 200000 and investment 500000: year-1 revenue = 2200000, EBIT = 280000, net income = 210000, working capital about 379726, so year-1 FCF is only about 274 because of the rise in working capital. Total NPV is about 2312443 and payback about 3.66 years; IRR with terminal value is about 60.79% and without it about 14.76%.

How to read the results

  • NPV card: "Profitable" (green) if NPV is above zero, otherwise "Loss-making". The value shown includes the terminal value.
  • IRR card: "> Discount Rate" (green) if IRR exceeds the discount rate, otherwise "≤ Discount Rate".
  • Payback Period and Terminal Value: in years and as an amount.
  • Projected Income Statement: per year revenue, COGS, operating expenses, depreciation, EBIT, tax and net income (negatives in red).
  • Free Cash Flows (FCF): net income, depreciation, CAPEX, change in WC and FCF per year.
  • Charts: a line chart of revenue and net income, a bar chart of free cash flow, then the "Project Valuation" card.

The code has no other rating thresholds. As general guidance: a positive NPV and an IRR above the discount rate support accepting the project; if most of the NPV comes from the terminal value, the result is very sensitive to the perpetual growth assumption.

Export

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with entity, date, currency and forecast period, base inputs, the KPI dashboard, charts, projected income statement, free cash flows and project valuation.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a workbook with 7 sheets: Report Cover, Inputs & Assumptions, KPI Dashboard, Projected Income Statement, Free Cash Flows, Charts, and Interpretation & Recommendations.

Export works after you click "Run Financial Forecast".

Tips and common mistakes

  • Initial working capital strongly affects year-1 FCF; if you leave it at zero, the whole calculated working capital is deducted from year-1 cash flow.
  • You cannot enter zero for the discount rate or perpetual growth: zero is replaced with 10% and 3% respectively. Use a small value such as 0.1 for near-zero perpetual growth.
  • Keep perpetual growth clearly below the discount rate (typically 2% to 4%); otherwise the terminal value is dropped.
  • Do not include depreciation in the operating-expense percentage, or it will be counted twice.
  • Run several scenarios (lower growth, higher costs) and compare NPV before deciding.

Additional help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (calculator button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (robot button) explains the steps for this tool.

name: Employee Evaluation Form
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

A job-performance evaluation form with 40 criteria across 8 domains. Each criterion is rated on a 1–5 scale, giving a total out of 200 points, an overall rating, a percentage for each domain and automatic development recommendations.

The question it answers: how well is this employee performing overall, and where are their strengths and the areas that need a development plan?

Use it for annual or half-year reviews, at the end of a probation period, before promotion, bonus or transfer decisions, or to build an individual development plan.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
CriterionCriterionA specific behaviour or skill the employee is rated on, such as "Punctuality and attendance".
DomainDomainA group of related criteria, such as "Work Commitment".
1–5 scaleRating scalePoor = 1, Average = 2, Good = 3, Very Good = 4, Excellent = 5.
Grade DateGrade DateThe date the employee obtained their current grade or job title.
Previous Evaluation ScorePrevious Evaluation ScoreResult of the last evaluation out of 100, shown in the report for comparison only.
Development planDevelopment PlanDated training and coaching actions to improve weak areas.

Before you start

  • Gather the employee data: work location, employee ID, name, qualification, job title, grade date, hire date and previous evaluation score.
  • Review attendance records, achievements and documented notes for the period so every rating rests on real examples.
  • This tool has no currency or entity-name field; the employee's name appears in the report and file name.

Filling in the data step by step

Employee Data

All these fields are optional and do not affect the calculation; an empty field shows as "Not entered" in the report.

FieldWhat to enterExample
Work LocationCity and branch or department.Istanbul, Beşiktaş branch
Employee IDThe employee number in the HR system.EMP-1024
Full NameThe employee's full name; also used in the Word file name.Sara Ahmed
QualificationHighest academic qualification.BSc Accounting
Job TitleCurrent position.Senior Accountant
Grade DateDate of the current grade or title (date picker).2024-01-01
Hire DateDate the employee joined the company.2019-09-15
Previous Evaluation ScoreLast evaluation result out of 100 (0 to 100); shown in the report for comparison and not used in the calculation.78

Performance Evaluation (40 criteria in 8 domains)

  1. Parent Company (4)
  2. Top Management (4)
  3. Department or Division (4)
  4. Specialization Area (4)
  5. Managerial Skills (4)
  6. Practical Skills (8)
  7. Work Commitment (6)
  8. Personal Traits & Relationships (6)
FieldWhat to chooseExample
Rating options for each criterionPick one of five: Poor (1), Average (2), Good (3), Very Good (4), Excellent (5). The counter and progress bar above the list show how many of the 40 criteria are answered.Punctuality and attendance → Very Good (4)

All 40 criteria must be answered; otherwise a warning appears and the form scrolls to the first unanswered criterion.

How the results are calculated

  • Total score = sum of the 40 criterion scores (40 to 200).
  • Overall % = total ÷ 200 × 100.
  • For each domain: domain % = sum of its scores ÷ (number of its criteria × 5) × 100.

All criteria carry equal weight, so "Practical Skills" (8 criteria) influences the total more than the four-criterion domains.

How to read the results

After "Show Results & Recommendations" a window shows the total in "points (out of 200)", the overall rating and its message, and the "Recommendations & Development" list. Overall rating thresholds in the code:

Overall %TotalRatingMessage
90% or more180–200ExcellentOutstanding performance, deserves recognition and promotion.
75% to below 90%150–179Very GoodHigh performance, with some areas for improvement.
60% to below 75%120–149GoodAcceptable performance, needs improvement in some areas.
45% to below 60%90–119AverageBelow expectations, needs a development plan.
Below 45%below 90PoorUnsatisfactory performance, requires urgent intervention.

After a general recommendation matching the rating, each domain gets a line based on its percentage: below 60% "weak" with a domain-specific development suggestion, 60% to below 75% "needs improvement" with a suggestion, and 75% or more "strong".

Export

Export requires all criteria to be answered.

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with all employee data, the total, rating and interpretation, recommendations and proposed development, and a detailed table per criterion (domain, criterion, rating, score).
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a workbook with 3 sheets: Report Cover (name, date, employee ID, work location, qualification, job title, previous evaluation), Results & Recommendations, and Evaluation Details.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Rate each criterion on documented examples from the period, not on a general impression or only the latest incident.
  • Avoid giving the same rating to every criterion; it makes the report useless for spotting development areas.
  • Some criteria may not apply to every role (for example "Relationship with subordinates" for someone with no reports); agree internally on a standard rating for such cases so comparisons stay fair.
  • Discuss the result and recommendations with the employee and turn "weak" domains into dated goals.
  • Enter the previous evaluation score so the comparison appears in the report.

Additional help

name: Managerial Assessment Scale
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

The "Managerial Assessment Scale" is a 26-statement self-assessment for managers and team leaders. It measures your "Retention Mindset": how well your beliefs and daily behaviour match what keeps talented employees engaged and willing to stay.

It answers the question: does the way I think as a manager help me keep my best people, or push them away? You get a score out of 104, a rating and development recommendations.

  • Before building a personal leadership development plan, or one for a group of managers.
  • When staff turnover rises or engagement drops.
  • Periodically (for example every 6 months) to track progress.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
Employee retentionEmployee RetentionThe organisation's ability to keep its competent employees and reduce resignations.
Retention mindsetRetention MindsetThe management beliefs and habits that make employees want to stay with you.
EngagementEmployee EngagementHow enthusiastic and committed an employee is, and how willing to go the extra mile.
MentoringMentoringA manager dedicating time to guide an employee and pass on experience to develop their career.
BurnoutBurnoutChronic physical and emotional exhaustion caused by work pressure, leading to lower performance and a wish to leave.
Incentive structureIncentive StructureThe system of financial and non-financial rewards linked to performance.
Self-assessmentSelf-AssessmentRating yourself honestly; the result is only useful if your answers are sincere.

Before you start

This tool needs no financial data and has no currency or entity-name field. Set aside about 10 minutes somewhere quiet and think about how you have actually behaved in recent months, not how you would like to behave.

Filling in the data step by step

The 26 statements are numbered, each with 4 options. Pick one option per statement; the counter (for example 12 / 26) and the progress bar update automatically, and the bar turns gold when everything is answered.

FieldWhat to enterExample
Options for each statement (1 to 26)Choose how much the statement applies to you: "Always / Yes" (1 point), "Usually / Often" (2), "Sometimes" (3), "Never / No" (4).Statement 13 "Do you feel you don't have time for mentoring?": if this is rarely true, choose "Sometimes" = 3 points.

When all statements are answered, click "Show Results & Recommendations". If any statement is unanswered, the message "Please answer all statements before viewing the result." appears and the page scrolls to the first missing statement, outlined in red.

How the results are calculated

Most statements describe beliefs that hinder retention, so "Never / No" earns the highest score. The calculation runs on the server:

  • Total score = sum of the 26 statement scores, each from 1 to 4; positive statement 14 is reversed (5 − answer). The Word report uses the same server score.
  • The minimum possible score is 26 and the maximum is 104.
  • The result is only calculated when every statement is answered.

Recommendations depend on the score: 2 for the Excellent level and 3 for each other level, plus an extra burnout recommendation if the score is 60 or less and an extra incentive-structure recommendation if it is 45 or less.

How to read the results

The "Assessment Result" window shows the score (for example 85 points (out of 104)), the rating, an explanatory message and the "Recommendations & Development" list. Rating thresholds used by the tool:

ScoreRatingMeaning
80 to 104Excellent - Talent Retention MindsetYour beliefs support keeping top talent; keep building trust and development.
53 to 79Moderate - Risk of Losing TalentYou risk losing your best employees; focus on communication and trust.
38 to 52Low - Urgent WarningHigh risk of losing talent; immediate, focused action is needed.
Below 38 (26 to 37)CriticalA fundamental leadership problem; an immediate change and intensive leadership coaching are recommended.

The higher the score, the better. Click "Got it ✓" or outside the window to close it.

Export

Exporting requires all statements to be answered. Available buttons:

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the total score, rating, interpretation, recommendations, a table of all 26 statements with the chosen answer and its score, and the report date.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a 3-sheet workbook: "Report Cover" (assessment, date, score, rating), "Results & Recommendations" and "Assessment Details" (statement number, statement, rating, score), where scores 3 and 4 appear in green, 2 in orange and 1 in red.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Answer honestly about your actual behaviour; "ideal" answers give a high score but do not help you improve.
  • Statement 14 is phrased positively ("Do you actually realize how much it costs you to lose…"), so it is reverse-scored: score = 5 − answer, i.e. "Always / Yes" = 4 points and "Never / No" = 1.
  • Focus on statements you answered with "Always / Yes" or "Usually / Often"; these are your development priorities.
  • Repeat the assessment 3 to 6 months after applying the recommendations and compare the two scores.
  • Ask a trusted colleague or your team to rate you on the same statements and compare their view with yours.

Additional help

name: Menu Engineering
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

"Menu Engineering" analyses every dish on your menu from two angles: profitability (how much each unit earns) and popularity (its share of total units sold). It then places each dish in one of 4 BCG-style categories with a practical recommendation.

It answers the question: which dishes should I promote, which should I re-price or make cheaper to produce, and which should I remove?

  • When redesigning or reprinting your menu.
  • When reviewing prices or recipe costs.
  • Monthly or quarterly to track dish performance after changes.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
BCGBoston Consulting Group MatrixA four-quadrant matrix that classifies items on two axes; here the axes are profitability and popularity.
Menu engineeringMenu EngineeringA method for deciding menu layout and prices based on each dish's profit and sales.
StarStarA dish with above-average profitability and popularity.
Question MarkQuestion MarkA profitable dish whose sales are below average.
Cash CowCash CowA dish that sells well but has a below-average margin.
DogDogA dish with below-average profitability and popularity.
Profit marginUnit Profit MarginSelling price minus dish cost, as a currency amount, not a percentage.
Popularity / Sales sharePopularity / Sales Share %The dish's units sold as a percentage of all units sold on the menu.

Before you start

  • Choose the "Currency:" and type the "Entity Name:" (restaurant or beneficiary); both appear on the exported report cover and in the file name.
  • For each dish collect: the current selling price, the cost of one portion (ingredients), and the number of units sold over the same period for all dishes (for example last month).
  • At least 2 dishes are needed for the analysis; ideally analyse one menu category at a time (starters only, mains only).

Filling in the data step by step

Add Dish

FieldWhat to enterExample
Dish NameThe dish name as it appears on the menu (required).Beef Burger
Selling PriceSelling price of one portion in the chosen currency; must be greater than zero.25.00
CostCost of preparing one portion (ingredients) in the currency; zero or more.12.50
Units SoldUnits sold during the period; a whole number, zero or more (decimals are dropped).150

Click "Add" or press Enter in any field to add the dish to the table; the fields are then cleared for the next dish. If data is missing or invalid, a message asks for "name, price >0, cost >=0, units >=0".

Import from Excel

FieldWhat to enterExample
Import from Excel:Choose an .xlsx or .xls file, then click "Import". Only the first sheet is read, using the first 4 columns in order: Name, Price, Cost, Units. A ready template is available via "Download Template".A header row, then: Beef Burger | 25 | 12.5 | 150

Invalid rows (such as the header row or a zero price) are skipped, and imported dishes are added to the existing ones. Remove a dish with the × button in the dishes table, or everything with "Clear All".

How the results are calculated

After you click "Analyze Menu & Extract Recommendations", the server calculates:

  • Profit margin = Selling price − Cost for each dish.
  • Weighted average margin = Σ (dish margin × units sold) ÷ Σ units sold (standard Kasavana & Smith method; if total units are zero, the simple average is used).
  • Sales share = (dish units ÷ total units of all dishes) × 100.
  • Popularity threshold = 70% × (100 ÷ number of dishes) (for example 17.5% for four dishes).
  • A dish is "profitable" if its margin ≥ the weighted average margin, and "popular" if its sales share ≥ the popularity threshold.
  • Revenue = Σ (price × units), Total cost = Σ (cost × units), Net profit = Revenue − Total cost.
  • If total units are zero, every dish gets a 0% share, so no dish counts as popular.

How to read the results

"Analysis Summary (BCG Matrix)" cards: total dishes, the number of Stars ⭐, Question Marks ❓, Cash Cows 🐄 and Dogs 🐕, total revenue and net profit (rounded to whole numbers).

"Profitability vs. Popularity Matrix": a scatter chart; the horizontal axis is "Popularity (Sales Share %)" and the vertical axis "Profit Margin (Currency)". Colours: green Star, yellow Question Mark, light blue Cash Cow, red Dog. Hover over a point to see the dish name.

"Recommendations Report": a table with Dish, Profit Margin, Sales Share, BCG Category and Recommendation. Classification rules:

CategoryConditionRecommendation in the tool
StarMargin ≥ average and sales share ≥ averageKeep promoting, maintain quality and keep the price stable.
Question MarkMargin ≥ average and sales share < averageImprove marketing, adjust the price or run promotions; invest cautiously.
Cash CowMargin < average and sales share ≥ averageRaise the price slightly or reduce cost to improve the margin.
DogMargin < average and sales share < averageConsider removing, redesigning or changing its ingredients.

"Net Profit" here is the dishes' profit before overheads (rent, salaries, etc.).

Export

Export buttons appear after the analysis:

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the entity name, date and currency, the dish count per category, revenue and net profit, the chart image, the per-dish recommendations table and a strategic summary of the categories.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a 6-sheet workbook: "Report Cover", "Inputs" (dishes with price, cost and units), "BCG Matrix" (margin, sales share, category, recommendation), "Summary" (category counts, revenue, costs, net profit), "Charts" (chart image) and "Recommendations" (one recommendation per category).

Tips and common mistakes

  • Use the same time period for every dish's sales, otherwise popularity shares will be misleading.
  • Enter the cost of one portion, not the cost of a whole batch or monthly purchases.
  • Analyse each menu category separately; comparing a dessert with a main course is not a fair comparison.
  • Any change to the dish list (add, delete, import) hides the previous results, so click the analyse button again.
  • Do not remove "Dogs" automatically; some have strategic value (a kids' or vegetarian dish, for example).

Additional help
