name: CAC & CLV Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

The "CAC & CLV Calculator" compares what you spend to win one new customer (CAC) with the profit that customer brings you over the whole relationship (CLV). It then calculates the ratio between them and gives you a rating and a recommendation.

It answers the question: is my marketing spend profitable, and does each new customer return more than they cost me?

  • When setting or increasing a marketing budget.
  • When comparing the results of one campaign with another.
  • When presenting a growth plan to investors or management.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
CACCustomer Acquisition CostThe average marketing spend needed to win one new customer.
CLVCustomer Lifetime ValueThe total profit expected from a customer over the years they buy from you. Also called LTV.
LTVLifetime ValueAnother name for CLV.
CLV / CACLifetime value to acquisition cost ratioHow many times a customer pays back their acquisition cost as profit; 3 or more is preferred.
Average order valueAverage Order Value (AOV)The average amount a customer spends per visit or purchase.
Profit marginProfit MarginThe percentage of each sale that remains as profit after costs.
Customer lifespanCustomer LifespanThe average number of years a customer keeps buying from you.

Before you start

  • Choose the "Currency:" and type the "Entity Name:"; both appear in the results, the exported reports and the file name.
  • From your accounts: marketing spend for one month (ads, promotions, commissions) and the number of new customers in that same month.
  • From sales records: average order value, how often a customer buys per year, how many years a customer stays, and your profit margin.

Filling in the data step by step

Input Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total Marketing Spend (Monthly)Everything spent on marketing in one month, in the chosen currency.5000
New Customers (Monthly)The number of new customers gained in the same month; a whole number.100
Average Order ValueThe average bill per visit, in the currency.25
Visits per Customer per YearHow many times a customer buys per year on average; decimals are allowed.12 or 1.5
Average Customer Lifespan (Years)Number of years; decimals are allowed.3 or 2.5
Profit Margin (%)Profit percentage of each sale; type 30 for 30% (not 0.30).30

Then click "Calculate CAC & CLV". All values must be greater than zero, otherwise the message "Please enter positive values for all fields." appears. An empty or zero field also shows this message.

How the results are calculated

The server calculates:

  • CAC = Total marketing spend ÷ New customers
  • Annual revenue per customer = Average order value × Visits per year
  • Lifetime revenue = Annual revenue × Lifespan (years)
  • CLV = Lifetime revenue × (Profit margin ÷ 100)
  • Ratio = CLV ÷ CAC

If new customers are zero, CAC is not calculated; if CAC is zero, the ratio is not calculated. In both cases «—» is shown instead of a misleading infinite number.

Example with the default values: CAC = 5000 ÷ 100 = 50 and CLV = 25 × 12 × 3 × 30% = 270, so the ratio is 5.40x.

How to read the results

"Summary Indicators" cards: Acquisition Cost (CAC), Lifetime Value (CLV), CLV / CAC Ratio (shown with an x) and Rating.

"Feasibility Analysis (CAC vs CLV)": a bar chart comparing CAC (red) with CLV (green); the taller the green bar, the better.

"Strategic Recommendations" and "Calculation Details": a recommendation based on the rating and a table (Indicator, Value, Explanation) covering all inputs and results. Rating thresholds used by the tool:

CLV / CAC ratioRatingMeaning
4 or moreExcellentExcellent, sustainable marketing strategy; look for expansion opportunities.
3 to below 4Very GoodMarketing investment is viable; improve it via higher order value or better retention.
2 to below 3ModerateReturn is not sufficient; review channels, costs or customer lifetime.
Below 2PoorMarketing is losing money; reduce CAC, raise prices or improve loyalty.

Export

Export buttons appear after the calculation:

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the entity name, date and currency, the four summary indicators, the chart image, the calculation details table and the strategic recommendation.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a 3-sheet workbook: "Report Cover" (entity, date, currency, ratio, rating), "CAC_CLV Details" (10 rows: indicator, value, explanation) and "Recommendations".

Tips and common mistakes

  • Use the same month for marketing spend and new customers; mixing periods distorts CAC.
  • Do not count returning customers as "New Customers".
  • Enter a realistic net or contribution margin, not a high gross margin, to avoid overstating CLV.
  • If you do not know the customer lifespan, start with a conservative estimate (1 or 2 years) and try different scenarios.
  • After changing any input, click the calculate button again before exporting; reports use the latest calculation.

Additional help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (calculator button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (robot button) explains the steps of this tool.

name: Analysis & Content Generation Tool
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

The "Analysis & Content Generation Tool" uses artificial intelligence to analyse text you paste (such as a report), prepare a weekly content plan, write complete content, or answer a question in detail.

It answers the question: how can I quickly get a structured analysis or ready-to-use content from an idea or a text I already have?

  • To summarise a long report and extract strengths, weaknesses and recommendations.
  • To plan a week of social media posts.
  • To write an article, an "about us" page or a detailed advisory answer.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
AIArtificial IntelligenceSoftware that generates text based on your instructions and the text you provide.
PromptPromptThe text you type in "Report Text or Details"; the clearer it is, the better the result.
Executive summaryExecutive SummaryA short opening paragraph summarising the key findings for decision makers.
Content planContent PlanA schedule of suggested ideas and posts for each day.
SectionSectionA part of the result that starts with a heading; each section is shown in its own card.

Before you start

This tool needs no currency or entity name. Prepare the text you want analysed, or a clear description of what you need: your business, target audience, desired tone and any key facts. The result is written in the current interface language (English when the site is in English).

Filling in the data step by step

Generation Settings

FieldWhat to enterExample
Service TypeChoose one of 4 services: "📊 Report Analysis" (executive summary, analysis, strengths/weaknesses, recommendations), "📅 Weekly Plan" (a content plan for a number of days), "🏗️ Build Full Content" (introduction, 3 sections, conclusion), "❓ Answer a Question" (a detailed answer).📅 Weekly Plan
CountShown only with "Weekly Plan": the number of days in the plan, a whole number from 1 to 30. Default 7.7
Report Text or DetailsPaste the report text or describe your request in detail (required). Only the first 8,000 characters are sent.Burger restaurant in Istanbul, audience: university students, youthful tone, goal: more evening orders.

Click "Start Analysis / Generation". If the field is empty, "Please enter the text." appears. While generating, a "Cancel Request" button lets you stop. The wait limit is 30 seconds, after which "Connection timeout" is shown.

How the results are calculated

There are no financial formulas in this tool. It sends the service type, count and your text to the server, which builds suitable instructions for each service, adds the output language and a request to use headings, and passes them to an AI model.

  • Links and promotional lines the model may add are removed from the result.
  • The text is split into cards at each heading.
  • Word Count = number of words separated by spaces, Character Count = length of the cleaned text, and Sections = number of parts produced when the text is split at headings.

How to read the results

After generation, 4 quick cards appear: Service Type, Word Count, Character Count and Sections. The "Generated Content" is then shown in cards, each with its heading and text.

The tool has no rating or numeric thresholds; the following is general guidance: always check figures and facts, because AI can make mistakes or invent information. If the result is too generic, add more detail to your request and generate again. The same request may give different results each time.

Export

The tool has a single export button, shown after generation:

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a Word file with the generated content as shown in the cards (headings and text) and the creation date. There is no Excel export in this tool.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Write a specific request: who you are, who your audience is, the goal, and the length and tone you want.
  • For "Report Analysis", paste the actual report text, not just its title, and avoid texts longer than 8,000 characters or split them.
  • Do not enter confidential or sensitive personal data in the request.
  • If you get a timeout or "Unexpected response from server", shorten the request and try again.
  • Review and edit the content before publishing; treat it as a good draft, not a final text.

Additional help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (calculator button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (robot button) explains the steps of this tool.

name: Cash Gap Calculator (CCC)
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

The "Cash Gap Calculator (CCC)" measures how many days your money stays tied up in inventory and receivables before it returns as cash, after subtracting the days your suppliers finance you.

It answers the question: for how many days do I need to finance my operating cycle with my own money or a loan?

  • When planning liquidity and working capital.
  • Before applying for financing or a credit line.
  • To compare collection, inventory and payment performance between periods.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
CCCCash Conversion Cycle (cash gap)Number of days between paying for goods and collecting cash from selling them.
DIODays Inventory OutstandingAverage number of days inventory is held before it is sold.
DSODays Sales OutstandingAverage number of days to collect money from customers.
DPODays Payables OutstandingAverage number of days before you pay suppliers.
COGSCost of Goods SoldThe cost of the goods sold during the period.
ReceivablesAccounts ReceivableAmounts customers owe you.
PayablesAccounts PayableAmounts you owe suppliers.

Before you start

  • Choose the currency from the currency list at the top of the page and enter the company or beneficiary name so it appears in exported reports.
  • Prepare the balance sheet at the start and end of the period (inventory, receivables, payables) and the income statement for the same period (COGS and credit sales).
  • Enter all amounts in the same currency, as plain numbers without separators or symbols.

Filling in the data step by step

Period Length

FieldWhat to enterExample
Period LengthChoose the period your income statement covers: Quarterly (3 months), Semi-Annual (6 months) or Annual (12 months, default).Annual (12 months)

Balance Sheet Data (Start and End of Period)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Beginning InventoryInventory value at the start of the period, in the selected currency.220000
Ending InventoryInventory value at the end of the period.280000
Beginning ReceivablesAmounts owed by customers at the start of the period.150000
Ending ReceivablesAmounts owed by customers at the end of the period.210000
Beginning PayablesAmounts owed to suppliers at the start of the period.100000
Ending PayablesAmounts owed to suppliers at the end of the period.140000

Income Statement Data (During the Period)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)Total cost of goods sold during the selected period. Must be greater than zero.1200000
Net Credit SalesSales made on credit, net of returns, during the period. Must be greater than zero.1500000

An empty field counts as zero. Then click "Calculate Cash Gap".

How the results are calculated

Days in period = months ÷ 12 × 365 (that is 91.25, 182.5 or 365 days).

  • Average = (beginning balance + ending balance) ÷ 2 for inventory, receivables and payables.
  • DIO = average inventory ÷ COGS × days in period
  • DSO = average receivables ÷ net credit sales × days in period
  • DPO = average payables ÷ COGS × days in period
  • CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO

Example with the default values (annual): DIO = 250000 ÷ 1200000 × 365 ≈ 76 days, DSO = 180000 ÷ 1500000 × 365 ≈ 43.8 days, DPO = 120000 ÷ 1200000 × 365 = 36.5 days, CCC ≈ 83.3 days.

How to read the results

You get 4 cards in days: DIO, DSO, DPO and the cash gap CCC with its status, two charts ("Cash Gap Components" and "Components Distribution"), "Calculation Details" and "Recommendations & Analysis". CCC rating:

CCC value (days)Rating
0 or lessExcellent (Negative Gap)
Above 0 up to 30Good (Short Gap)
Above 30 up to 60Moderate (Moderate Gap)
Above 60 up to 90High (Long Gap)
Above 90Critical (Very Long Gap)

CCC card colour: green up to 30 days, yellow up to 60, red above that. Extra recommendations are added when DIO is above 45 days (slow inventory), DSO is above 45 days (slow collection) or DPO is below 30 days (paying suppliers quickly).

Export

The export buttons appear after calculation:

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the entity name, date, currency, period length, an inputs table with averages, the indicators table, the rating and an image of the charts.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a 6-sheet workbook: Report Cover, Inputs & Assumptions, KPI Dashboard, Calculation Details, Charts, Interpretation & Recommendations (inventory advice together with the DSO collection and DPO payment advice).

Tips and common mistakes

  • Use only credit sales in "Net Credit Sales"; entering total cash and credit sales makes DSO look lower than it really is.
  • Make sure the period length matches the income statement period; a full year of COGS with "Quarterly" selected greatly understates the days.
  • Do not leave COGS or credit sales empty; the calculation stops unless both are greater than zero.
  • To shorten the gap: turn inventory over faster, collect from customers sooner and negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers.
  • Compare the result with your industry average; a normal gap differs between retail, manufacturing and services.

Additional help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (calculator button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (robot button) explains the steps of this tool.

name: Investment Analysis (NPV / IRR / Payback)
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

"Investment Analysis (NPV / IRR / Payback)" evaluates whether an investment project is worthwhile by comparing the amount invested today with the cash flows expected in future years, discounted at your required rate of return.

It answers the question: is this project worth investing in, and when will I get my capital back?

  • Before buying equipment, opening a branch or launching a new product.
  • To choose between two or more projects.
  • To prepare a feasibility study for an investor or bank.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
NPVNet Present ValueSum of cash flows discounted to today minus the initial investment.
IRRInternal Rate of ReturnThe discount rate at which NPV equals zero; the project’s actual annual return.
PaybackPayback PeriodYears needed to recover the investment from ordinary cash flows.
Discounted PaybackDiscounted Payback PeriodYears needed to recover the investment from discounted cash flows.
WACCWeighted Average Cost of CapitalThe minimum required return, used here as the discount rate.
Discount factorDiscount FactorThe number a year’s cash flow is multiplied by to convert it to today’s value.
Cash flowCash FlowNet cash coming in during the year (cash receipts minus cash expenses).

Before you start

  • Choose the currency from the currency list at the top of the page and enter the company or beneficiary name so it appears in exported reports.
  • Prepare the initial investment amount, the required discount rate and an estimate of net cash flow for each project year.
  • A 5-year example is loaded automatically when the page opens; replace its values with your data.

Filling in the data step by step

Project Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Initial InvestmentAmount paid at the start of the project in the selected currency; must be greater than zero.500000
Discount Rate (WACC) (%)A percentage: type 12 for 12%, not 0.12. Required: an empty or negative value shows the validation message; type 0 explicitly if you want a zero rate.12
Project Duration (Years)Number of cash flow years, a whole number from 1 to 50. Changing it updates the year rows immediately and keeps the values already typed; you can also use "Add Year" and "Remove Last Year".5

Annual Cashflows

FieldWhat to enterExample
Year 1, Year 2, ...Expected net cash flow for each year in the selected currency. A negative value can be entered for a loss year. An empty field counts as zero.150000

"Add Year" adds a new row and increases the duration, "Remove Last Year" deletes the last row (at least one row remains), and "Load Example" fills 5 years: 150000, 180000, 220000, 200000, 180000. Then click "Calculate Investment Metrics". Invalid values show "Please enter valid values (Investment > 0, Discount Rate >= 0, Years > 0).".

How the results are calculated

  • Discount factor for year t = 1 ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate.
  • NPV = − initial investment + Σ cash flow of year t ÷ (1 + r)^t
  • IRR: the rate that makes NPV = 0, found with the Newton-Raphson method starting at 10%, up to 1,000 iterations, tolerance 0.00001, limited to −99% to 1000%; if it does not converge, bisection is used. If the cash flows never change sign (all positive or all negative), no IRR exists and «—» is shown. Check: investment 100000 with flows 30000 / 35000 / 40000 / 45000 at 10% → NPV = 16986.54 and IRR = 17.09%.
  • Payback = year in which the cumulative total reaches the investment − (excess ÷ that year’s cash flow)
  • Discounted payback uses the same method on discounted cash flows. If the investment is not recovered within the project duration, ∞ is shown.

Example with the default values: investment 500000, discount 12%; the ordinary cumulative total reaches 550000 in year 3, so payback ≈ 3 − 50000 ÷ 220000 ≈ 2.77 years.

How to read the results

You get cards for NPV (✅ Positive or ❌ Negative), IRR compared with the discount rate, Payback in years, Discounted Payback and the Final Verdict. Then an "Annual Cashflow" chart with a "Cumulative" line, a table with year, cash flow, discount factor (4 decimals), discounted value and discounted cumulative (starting at minus the investment), and a "Recommendations & Analysis" box.

ConditionFinal Verdict
NPV greater than 0 and IRR greater than the discount rateAcceptable (Viable Investment)
Only one of the two conditions is metPartially Acceptable (Review)
Neither condition is metNot Acceptable (Non-Viable)

The recommendations also compare the payback period with the project duration: shorter is good, and if it exceeds the duration a ⚠️ warning is shown.

Export

The export buttons appear after calculation:

  • Blue button "Full Word Export": a report with the entity name, date, currency, inputs, each year’s cash flow, the indicators and the chart.
  • Green button "Full Excel Export": a 6-sheet workbook: Report Cover, Inputs & Assumptions, Cashflows, KPI Dashboard (NPV, IRR, Payback, Verdict), Charts, Recommendations.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Enter the discount rate as a percentage (12, not 0.12); otherwise 0.12% is used and the project looks far better than it is.
  • Enter net cash flow, not just revenue; subtract cash expenses and taxes.
  • Reducing "Project Duration (Years)" removes the last year rows and their values, so review the cash flows after any duration change.
  • Rely on NPV first when comparing projects of different sizes; IRR alone can mislead.
  • Try different discount rates to see how sensitive the result is.

Additional help

Hover over any field to see its explanation; the side calculator (calculator button) can insert its result into the selected field, and the smart assistant (robot button) explains the steps of this tool.

name: Startup Software Company Valuation
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool estimates a valuation range (Low, Base and High) for a startup software company, especially a SaaS business. It answers the question: what is the company worth today, and how healthy are the metrics investors look at?

It works in two stages, selected with the buttons at the top of the form:

  • Post-Revenue: the company has recurring revenue. The value is estimated with a revenue multiple (set by a scoring model based on your metrics) and the Venture Capital (VC) method, alongside SaaS metrics such as the Rule of 40, LTV/CAC, Magic Number, Burn Multiple and Runway.
  • Pre-Revenue: the company is not selling yet. The value is estimated with the Berkus Method and the Replacement Cost Method.

Use it before a funding round, when negotiating with an investor or partner, or to monitor your metrics regularly.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
SaaSSoftware as a ServiceSoftware sold through a recurring subscription instead of a one-off licence.
ARRAnnual Recurring RevenueRecurring subscription and contract revenue expressed on a yearly basis.
MRRMonthly Recurring RevenueARR divided by 12; used internally to calculate CAC payback.
YoYYear over YearThis year's figure compared with last year's.
NRRNet Revenue RetentionRevenue kept from existing customers after one year, including upgrades and cancellations; above 100% means existing customers pay more.
ChurnChurn RateShare of customers who cancel each month.
CACCustomer Acquisition CostAverage sales and marketing spend to win one new customer.
LTVCustomer Lifetime ValueTotal revenue expected from a customer over the whole relationship.
LTV/CACLifetime Value to Acquisition Cost ratioHow many times a customer pays back what it cost to acquire them.
CAC PaybackCAC payback periodMonths needed to recover CAC from the customer's gross profit.
Rule of 40Rule of 40Growth rate plus operating margin; 40% or more signals a good balance between growth and profitability.
Magic NumberSaaS Magic NumberSales and marketing efficiency: new annual revenue generated per unit of spend.
Net BurnNet Burn RateNet cash going out each month (expenses minus revenue).
Burn MultipleBurn MultipleCash burned for each unit of new ARR; lower is better.
RunwayCash RunwayNumber of months the current cash lasts at the current burn.
VCVenture CapitalInvestors who fund startups for equity and target a multiple of their money at exit.
ROIReturn on InvestmentHere: the target return multiple, i.e. how many times the investor wants their money back.
ExitExitSale or IPO of the company, when investors realise their return.
EVEnterprise ValueValue of the whole company as estimated by the revenue multiple.
Berkus MethodBerkus MethodPre-revenue valuation that assigns a value to each of five qualitative elements, up to the «Max per element» field (default 500,000 in the selected currency).
Replacement CostReplacement Cost MethodWhat it would cost to rebuild the same product from scratch, plus a risk premium.
MVPMinimum Viable ProductThe simplest version of the product that can be tested with customers.
KPIKey Performance IndicatorA number that measures an important aspect of performance.

Before you start

  • Choose the currency in Currency: and type the Company Name:; both appear in the exported reports.
  • Select the stage: Post-Revenue or Pre-Revenue. Switching stage hides previous results.
  • For Post-Revenue, gather: current ARR, annual growth, gross and operating margins, monthly churn, NRR, customer count, CAC, LTV, net monthly burn, cash on hand, ideally the last two quarters of ARR and sales and marketing spend, and your exit assumptions.
  • For Pre-Revenue: your estimate for each of the five Berkus elements and the cost to rebuild the technology.
  • All amounts are in the selected currency.

Filling in the data step by step

All percentages are typed as whole numbers: 50 means 50% (do not type 0.5).

Post-Revenue: Revenue & Growth

FieldWhat to enterExample
Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)Current annual recurring revenue in the selected currency.1000000
Annual Growth Rate (%)Revenue growth versus last year, as a percentage; negative values are allowed.50
Gross Margin (%)(Revenue − cost of delivering the service) ÷ revenue, as a percentage.75
Operating Profit Margin (%)Operating profit ÷ revenue, as a percentage; may be negative.-10
Monthly Churn Rate (%)Share of customers cancelling per month.2
Net Revenue Retention NRR (%)Revenue from existing customers now ÷ their revenue a year ago, as a percentage. If left empty, 100 is used.110

Post-Revenue: Unit Economics

FieldWhat to enterExample
Current CustomersNumber of paying customers today; used to compute monthly revenue per customer.200
Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)Average sales and marketing cost per new customer (amount).5000
Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)Average revenue expected from a customer over the relationship (amount).25000
Net Monthly BurnNet monthly cash outflow = expenses − revenue (monthly amount). Enter 0 if the company is not burning cash.40000
Cash on HandTotal cash in the company's accounts today.500000

Post-Revenue: Advanced Metrics (Optional for accuracy)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Current Quarter ARRARR at the end of the current quarter.1000000
Previous Quarter ARRARR at the end of the previous quarter.900000
Sales & Marketing (Prev Quarter)Total sales and marketing spend in the previous quarter (quarterly amount).120000

The exact Magic Number is used only when all three fields are filled and both the spend and the previous quarter ARR are above zero; otherwise a note says the value is estimated.

Post-Revenue: Venture Capital (VC) Method

FieldWhat to enterExample
Expected Exit ValueExpected value of the company at sale or IPO in a few years (amount).50000000
Target ROI MultipleHow many times the investor wants their money back (a multiple, not a percentage). Empty or zero is treated as 10.10
Exit YearsExpected years until exit (3 to 10). Used to calculate the investor’s implied annual return in the VC method.6

Pre-Revenue: Berkus Method

FieldWhat to enterExample
Idea & Solution QualityValue you assign to the idea's innovation and market fit, 0 up to the max per element.350000
Prototype & TechnologyValue of having a prototype or scalable technology, up to the max per element.400000
Founding Team StrengthValue of the founders' experience and track record, up to the max per element.450000
Strategic RelationshipsValue of partnerships, distribution channels and investor relationships, up to the max per element.200000
Execution & Early SalesValue of any early sales or customer commitments, up to the max per element.250000
FieldWhat to enterExample
Max per elementHighest value any Berkus element can take, in the selected currency (the original method uses USD 500,000; adjust it to your market and currency).500000

Any value above the max is reduced to it in the calculation.

Pre-Revenue: Replacement Cost Method

FieldWhat to enterExample
Technology Rebuild CostCost to build the product and technology from scratch today (amount).300000
Risk Premium (%)Extra percentage for market, competition and execution risk.25

Then click Calculate Valuation Range.

How the results are calculated

Post-Revenue stage

  • Rule of 40: Rule40 = growth rate + operating margin
  • LTV/CAC = LTV ÷ CAC (zero if CAC is zero).
  • Monthly revenue per customer: MRR per customer = (ARR ÷ 12) ÷ customers
  • Payback in months: CAC Payback = CAC ÷ (MRR per customer × gross margin ÷ 100); shows N/A if customers or CAC is zero.
  • Exact Magic Number: Magic = ((current quarter ARR − previous quarter ARR) × 4) ÷ sales & marketing spend. Estimated (no quarterly data): Magic = (ARR × growth ÷ 100) ÷ (net burn × 12 × 0.6), or zero if growth or burn is zero or negative.
  • Net new ARR: ARR × growth ÷ 100; Burn Multiple: (net burn × 12) ÷ net new ARR (N/A if either is zero or negative).
  • Runway in months: Runway = cash on hand ÷ net burn; if burn is zero it shows ∞.

Scoring model (maximum 100 points) that sets the revenue multiple:

MetricPoints
Growth100% or more: 40; 50% to under 100%: 30 + (growth − 50) × 0.2; 20% to under 50%: 15 + (growth − 20) × 0.5; under 20%: growth × 0.75
Gross margin80% or more: 15; 60% to under 80%: 10 + (margin − 60) × 0.25; under 60%: 0
NRR130% or more: 15; 100% to under 130%: 10 + (NRR − 100) × 0.166; under 100%: 0
Monthly churn1% or less: 10; up to 2%: 8; up to 5%: 4; above 5%: 0
LTV/CAC5 or more: 10; 3 to under 5: 6 + (ratio − 3) × 2; 1 to under 3: ratio × 2; under 1: 0
Rule of 4040 or more: 10; 0 to under 40: value × 0.25; negative: 0
  • Base multiple: Base multiple = 2 + (score ÷ 100) × 18 (2x to 20x).
  • Low multiple = the higher of 1.5 and (base − 2.2); High multiple = the lower of 22 and (base + 2.2).
  • Revenue multiple valuation: Low/Base/High = ARR × matching multiple
  • VC method: Base = exit value ÷ target ROI multiple; Low = Base × 0.7; High = Base × 1.4. The tool also shows implied annual IRR = ROI multiple^(1 ÷ exit years) − 1; e.g. 10x over 6 years = 46.78% a year.
  • Overall range: Low = lowest of the two Low values; Base = average of the two Base values; High = highest of the two High values.

Pre-Revenue stage

  • Berkus value = sum of the five elements, each capped at the max per element.
  • Risk-adjusted replacement cost: rebuild cost × (1 + risk premium ÷ 100)
  • Range: Low = the smaller of the two values, Base = their average, High = the larger.

How to read the results

Post-Revenue

  • KPI cards: ARR (in thousands, K), Growth Rate, NRR, LTV/CAC, CAC Payback, Magic Number, Burn Multiple, Runway.
  • Rule of 40 badge: below 20%: red; 20% to under 40%: warning; 40% or more: green, Achieved.
  • Valuation Range table (in millions, M): Revenue Multiple row, VC Method row and Overall Range row.
  • Valuation Chart: bars for both methods at the three levels.
  • Interpretation, using these thresholds from the code:
MetricGood when
Rule of 4040% or more
LTV/CAC3x or more
CAC Paybackunder 12 months
Magic Number1 or more
Burn Multipleunder 1.5x
Runwaymore than 18 months (the same on screen and in the Word and Excel reports)
Growth rate (reports)above 20%
NRR (reports)100% or more

Pre-Revenue

You see Berkus Value and Replacement Cost cards (in thousands, K) and a table with both values and the Overall Range; there is no chart. Early-stage valuation is subjective by nature.

Export

  • Full Word Export (blue button): a report with a cover (company, date, stage, currency), a colour-coded KPI table (green good, red needs improvement), the valuation range table, the metric interpretation and, for Post-Revenue, the chart.
  • Full Excel Export (green button): a workbook with 6 sheets for Post-Revenue: Report Cover, Inputs, KPI Dashboard, Valuation Range, Chart, Interpretation & Recommendations. Pre-Revenue has 5 sheets (no Chart sheet).

Click Calculate Valuation Range before exporting.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Type percentages as whole numbers (2 means 2%), not decimals.
  • Churn here is monthly; if you only have an annual rate, divide it roughly by 12.
  • Fill in all three quarterly fields to get an exact Magic Number instead of an estimate.
  • Make sure net burn is monthly, not annual, or Runway will look far too short.
  • Exit value and target ROI multiple drive the VC method directly; try several scenarios.
  • In Berkus, do not exceed the max per element; higher values do not raise the valuation.

name: Scenario Analysis
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool simulates how changes in three key drivers affect monthly profitability: sales, salaries and raw material costs. It answers the what-if question: what happens to net profit and profit margin if, for example, sales fall 20% and salaries rise 15%?

Use it when preparing a budget, before deciding on pay rises or price changes, or when you expect material prices to rise or the market to slow, so you know the impact before it happens.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
ScenarioScenarioAn assumption about a possible future change in sales or costs.
What-if analysisWhat-If AnalysisChanging inputs to see their effect on the result.
Current (base case)Base CaseToday's actual monthly figures before any change.
Total CostsTotal CostsSalaries + raw materials + other operating expenses.
Net ProfitNet ProfitRevenue minus total costs.
Profit MarginProfit MarginNet profit as a percentage of revenue.
Percentage pointPercentage pointThe direct difference between two percentages; a margin moving from 34% to 21% is −13 percentage points.
KPIKey Performance IndicatorA number that measures an important aspect of performance; shown in the KPI Dashboard sheet of the Excel report.

Before you start

  • Choose the currency in Currency: and type the Entity Name:; both appear in the reports.
  • Prepare the figures for a typical month: revenue, salaries, raw materials and other operating expenses.
  • Decide the percentage changes you want to test for sales, salaries and raw materials.

Filling in the data step by step

Base Financial Data (monthly amounts in the selected currency)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Monthly RevenueTotal sales in a typical month; must be above zero.500000
Monthly SalariesTotal monthly salaries and wages; zero or more.150000
Raw Material CostCost of raw materials used per month; zero or more.100000
Other Operating ExpensesAll other monthly expenses (rent, utilities, marketing...); zero or more. They stay fixed in the scenario.80000

Scenario Changes (Percentage Values)

Type the change as a percentage: 15 means a 15% increase and -20 means a 20% decrease. An empty field counts as zero (no change).

FieldWhat to enterExample
Sales: Change %Expected change in monthly revenue.-20
Salaries: Change %Expected change in monthly salaries.15
Raw Materials: Change %Expected change in raw material cost.10

Then click Run Simulation. If revenue is zero or any cost is negative, a message asks for valid values.

How the results are calculated

  • Current: Total Costs = Salaries + Raw Materials + Other Costs, Net Profit = Revenue − Total Costs, Profit Margin = Net Profit ÷ Revenue × 100
  • Scenario: Scenario Revenue = Revenue × (1 + sales change ÷ 100), and the same for salaries and raw materials. Other costs do not change.
  • Scenario Costs = scenario salaries + scenario materials + other costs; scenario profit and margin are then calculated as above (margin is zero if scenario revenue is zero or less).
  • Change = scenario value − current value for each line; the margin change is in percentage points, and % change = change ÷ |current value| × 100 (absolute value, so the sign does not flip when current profit is negative); «—» is shown when the current value is zero. Example: current profit −10,000 and scenario +5,000 → change +15,000 = +150%.
  • The scenario is considered better when scenario net profit is greater than current net profit.

How to read the results

  • Cards: scenario Revenue, Total Costs, Net Profit and Profit Margin, each with the change underneath. Green means a change in your favour (higher revenue, profit or margin, or lower costs); red means the opposite.
  • Charts: Current vs Scenario shows bars for revenue, total costs and net profit (scenario bars are green if profit improves, red if it falls); Scenario Impact on Margin & Profit shows margin and profit before and after.
  • Detailed Comparison Table: current value, scenario value, change and change % for each line.
  • Recommendations & Analysis: if profit improves, the improvement is shown; if it falls, the main reasons are listed (revenue decline, salary increase, raw material cost increase) with a recommendation to review the cost structure.

The tool has no fixed rating thresholds for margin. As general guidance, watch the margin if it approaches zero or turns negative, which means the scenario pushes the business into a loss. The profit change % is measured against current profit, so it is misleading when current profit is negative or close to zero.

Export

  • Full Word Export (blue button): a report with a cover (entity, date, currency), the scenario changes, the comparison table, the conclusion and the chart images.
  • Full Excel Export (green button): a workbook with 6 sheets: Report Cover, Inputs & Assumptions, KPI Dashboard, Comparison Table, Charts, Recommendations.

Run the simulation before exporting.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Use monthly figures in all base fields; do not mix monthly and annual numbers.
  • Type -20 for a decrease, not 20; the minus sign is what makes it a decrease.
  • Try several scenarios (optimistic, expected, pessimistic) and export a report for each to compare.
  • Other costs are fixed in the simulation; if you expect them to change, edit the base value directly.
  • If current profit is negative, focus on the amounts rather than the profit change %.

Extra help

name: Knowledge & Personal Skills Assessment
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

A self-assessment that measures your level in the financial and management knowledge and skills a manager or team leader needs, using 16 criteria across 4 domains: Knowledge, Capabilities, Directions and Behaviors (4 criteria each).

It answers the question: what is my true level, and which critical areas should I develop first? Weak areas are colour-coded as you answer.

Use it when building a personal development plan, before an annual performance review, or to identify training needs for an employee or a team.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
KPIKey Performance IndicatorA number that shows how well an important goal is being met, such as sales growth.
HRHuman ResourcesThe function responsible for payroll, hiring and career development.
DCFDiscounted Cash FlowValuing a project or company by discounting its future cash flows to today's value.
Income StatementIncome StatementRevenue, expenses and net profit over a period.
Balance SheetBalance SheetAssets, liabilities and equity on a given date.
Cash FlowCash Flow StatementCash coming in and going out over a period.
Management AccountingManagement AccountingCost and budget information managers use to make decisions.
Business caseBusiness CaseA written argument that justifies a project with figures, benefits and risks.
Financial ratiosFinancial RatiosMeasures such as profitability and liquidity calculated from financial statements for comparison.
Critical itemCritical itemA criterion scored 0 or 1; shown in red.
Warning itemWarning itemA criterion scored 2; shown in orange.

Before you start

  • This tool has no currency; the personal details are what appear in the report.
  • Enter Full Name, Job Title and Department, and choose the Assessment Date (if left empty, today's date is used in the report).
  • Set aside quiet time and answer honestly; the value of the assessment is its accuracy, not a high score.

Filling in the data step by step

Personal details

FieldWhat to enterExample
Full NameName of the person being assessed.Ahmed Ali
Job TitleCurrent position.Sales Manager
DepartmentDepartment or unit they work in.Sales
Assessment DateDate of the assessment, from the date picker.2026-11-18

The 16 criteria

For each criterion choose one score from 0 to 5:

ScoreMeaning
0Unaware
1Minimal Knowledge
2Reasonable Familiarity
3Good Level
4Above Average
5Expert
DomainWhat its four criteria measure
KnowledgeUnderstanding financial statements, using discounted cash flows, management accounting, HR policies.
CapabilitiesAnalysing a company website within 10 minutes, calculating financial ratios against industry standards, optimistic/realistic/pessimistic estimates, presenting a business case and adjusting KPIs.
DirectionsSpending prudently, moving toward KPIs and changing them when needed, commitment to goals, seeing financial management as support for goals.
BehaviorsFollowing financial news and the industry, one-on-one talks with the team, reviewing the personal development plan, enthusiasm and determination to hit KPIs.

The progress bar shows how many of the 16 criteria are answered. Then click Show Results & Recommendations; if a criterion is unanswered, a warning appears and the page scrolls to it.

How the results are calculated

  • Total score = sum of the 16 criterion scores (0 to 80).
  • Percentage = score ÷ 80 × 100; the rating is based on this.
  • Every criterion scored 0 or 1 is listed under critical areas; every criterion scored 2 under concerning areas.
  • The result is calculated only after all criteria are answered.

How to read the results

A window shows the score out of 80, the rating, an explanatory message and the recommendations. The rating per the code:

Percentage (points)Rating
85% or more (68 points or more)Expert Practitioner
70% to under 85% (56 to 67)Advanced
50% to under 70% (40 to 55)Qualified
30% to under 50% (24 to 39)Beginner
Under 30% (under 24)Limited Awareness
  • Recommendations list critical areas (red) first, then concerning areas (orange); if there are none, a "no critical areas" message is shown.
  • A closing tip is added by percentage: under 50%: build financial and management knowledge through courses and mentoring; 50% to under 70%: deepen the orange areas and practise them on real projects; 70% or more: share your knowledge and take on leadership roles.
  • While you answer, a criterion turns red when you choose 0 or 1 and orange when you choose 2.

Export

  • Full Word Export (blue button): a report with the personal details, score out of 80 and rating, recommendations and a criteria table (number, domain, criterion, rating, score).
  • Full Excel Export (green button): a workbook with 3 sheets: Report Cover, Results & Recommendations, Assessment Details.

You can export before answering every criterion, but the report will show the result as Incomplete.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Rate what you actually do today, not what you intend to do.
  • Ask a colleague or your manager to rate you as well, then compare the two results.
  • Start your development plan with the red criteria, then the orange ones.
  • Repeat the assessment about every 6 months to track progress, and keep the reports for comparison.

name: Restaurant Valuation Calculator
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

This tool calculates the fair value of a restaurant or small food business using an EBITDA multiple minus debt, then works out the value of your share based on your ownership, the payback period and an efficiency index against the value of the equipment.

It answers the question: what is the restaurant worth today, what is my share worth, and does it create more value than its assets? It automatically accounts for the risk of a lease that is about to expire and lets you test the effect of an additional capital injection.

Use it when buying or selling a restaurant, when a partner joins or leaves, when negotiating a stake, or before an expansion decision.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
EBITDAEarnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and AmortizationThe restaurant's cash operating profit before financing costs, taxes and depreciation; here = Revenue − COGS − OPEX.
COGSCost of Goods SoldCost of the raw materials and ingredients used in the dishes sold.
OPEXOperating ExpensesRent, salaries, utilities, marketing and similar costs.
D&ADepreciation and AmortizationThe annual accounting decline in the value of equipment and assets.
EVEnterprise ValueValue of the whole restaurant before deducting debt = EBITDA × multiple.
Fair ValueFair Value (Equity Value)What is left for the owners after deducting debt from EV; never below zero.
Market MultipleMarket MultipleThe number EBITDA is multiplied by to estimate value; between 2 and 4 for restaurants in this tool.
Payback PeriodPayback PeriodYears needed to recover the fair value from net profit.
Efficiency IndexEfficiency IndexFair value divided by the value of equipment and furniture; 1 or more means operations create value above the assets.
Capital InjectionCapital InjectionAn extra amount invested in the restaurant for an expected annual return.
ROIReturn on InvestmentThe expected annual return on the injected amount, as a percentage.
Sensitivity AnalysisSensitivity AnalysisShowing how the value changes when the multiple changes.
KPIKey Performance IndicatorA number that measures an important aspect of performance; shown in the KPI Dashboard sheet of the Excel report.

Before you start

  • Choose the currency in Currency: and type the Restaurant Name:; both appear in the reports.
  • Prepare the financial statements for the last full year: revenue, COGS, operating expenses, depreciation, interest, taxes and outstanding debt.
  • Know the lease expiry year, estimate what the equipment and furniture would sell for today, and your ownership percentage.

Filling in the data step by step

Basic Restaurant Data

FieldWhat to enterExample
Establishment YearYear the restaurant started trading (1990 to 2026). Shown in the Excel inputs sheet; not used in the calculation.2018
Lease Expiry YearYear the premises lease ends (2025 to 2050). If fewer than 3 years remain, the multiplier is reduced automatically.2029

Financial Data (Annual)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Total RevenueAnnual restaurant sales (amount).500000
Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)Annual cost of raw materials and ingredients.200000
Operating Expenses (OPEX)Annual rent, salaries, utilities, marketing, excluding depreciation, interest and taxes.150000
Depreciation & Amortization (D&A)Annual depreciation of equipment and assets.20000
Interest PaidAnnual interest on loans.10000
Taxes PaidTotal annual taxes.15000
Total Outstanding DebtRemaining balance of all loans today.200000
Equipment & Furniture Market ValueEstimated price if the equipment and furniture were sold today.80000
Market Multiple (2 - 4)A number from 2 to 4 reflecting brand strength and profit growth: 2 for an ordinary restaurant, 4 for a strong brand with clear growth. Empty is treated as 3.3

Capital Injection Scenario (optional)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Enable InjectionTick to enable the two injection fields and include them in the calculation.Ticked
Injection AmountThe extra amount to be invested.50000
Expected ROI (%)Expected annual return on the injection as a percentage: 20 means 20%. Empty is treated as 20.20

Your Share in the Restaurant

FieldWhat to enterExample
Ownership Percentage (%)The share of the restaurant you own (1 to 100): 50 means 50%. Empty is treated as 100.50

Then click Calculate Valuation.

How the results are calculated

  • EBITDA = Revenue − COGS − OPEX
  • Net Profit = EBITDA − D&A − Interest − Taxes
  • Lease adjustment: Remaining = lease expiry year − current year. Lease factor = 1 with 3 or more years left; max(0.2, remaining ÷ 3) with less than 3 years; 0.2 if the lease has expired. Then Adjusted multiple = multiple × lease factor, so the multiple declines gradually with no jumps. Check (EBITDA 130,000, multiple 3, debt 100,000, year 2026): expiry 2030 → 350,000; 2028 → multiple 2.00, value 200,000; 2027 → 1.00 and 50,000; 2026 → 0.60 and 0.
  • Enterprise Value (EV) = EBITDA × adjusted multiple
  • Fair Value = EV − total debt; shown as zero if negative.
  • Your Share Price = Fair Value × ownership ÷ 100
  • Payback Period = Fair Value ÷ Net Profit in years; Infinite if net profit is zero or negative.
  • Efficiency Index = Fair Value ÷ equipment and furniture market value (zero if no asset value is entered).
  • With injection enabled: Extra EBITDA = injection × ROI ÷ 100, New fair value = (EBITDA + extra) × adjusted multiple − debt, New payback = new fair value (not below zero) ÷ (net profit + extra).
  • Sensitivity analysis: for each multiple 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 and 4: EV = EBITDA × multiple, fair value = EV − debt (not below zero), and the share price by ownership. The table applies the same lease factor to each multiple and is also included in the Word report.

How to read the results

  • Cards: EBITDA, Enterprise Value (EV) with the multiple used, Fair Value (Positive and green if above zero; it is already net of debt), Your Share Price, Payback Period and Efficiency Index.
  • Efficiency Index: 1 or more: Viable; below 1: Non-viable. The comparison card says the restaurant generates value above its assets when fair value is greater than or equal to the asset value; otherwise it is not operationally viable.
  • Lease warning: appears when fewer than 3 years remain on the lease (with the adjusted multiple) or when the lease has expired.
  • After capital injection: expected fair value and new payback period, if injection is enabled.
  • Sensitivity Analysis table: shows the negotiation range between a multiple of 2 and 4.
  • In the Excel KPI Dashboard sheet a metric is marked good when: EBITDA is above zero, fair value and share price are above zero, payback is under 10 years, the efficiency index is 1 or more, and the multiple used is 2 or more.

Export

  • Full Word Export (blue button): a report with the key indicators table (EBITDA, fair value, share price, payback period, efficiency index, multiple used), the lease warning if any, the capital injection impact if enabled, and the recommendation.
  • Full Excel Export (green button): a workbook with 5 sheets: Report Cover, Inputs & Assumptions, KPI Dashboard, Sensitivity Analysis, Recommendations.

Click Calculate Valuation before exporting.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Do not put rent or salaries in COGS; they belong in operating expenses (OPEX).
  • Do not include depreciation, interest or taxes in OPEX; they are deducted separately to reach net profit.
  • A lease with fewer than 3 years left cuts the valuation sharply; renew it before selling if you can.
  • Use the sensitivity table to set a floor price (multiple 2) and an ambitious price (multiple 4) in negotiations.
  • If fair value is zero, debt exceeds enterprise value; review debt and costs.

Extra help

name: 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

An operational tool that forecasts your cash balance week by week for 13 weeks (about one quarter), starting from your current balance and the weekly receipts and payments you expect.

It answers the question: will there be enough cash to meet obligations over the coming weeks, and in exactly which week might a deficit occur or the balance fall below the safe minimum?

Use it weekly to manage short-term liquidity, before scheduling supplier payments, when negotiating short-term financing, or during periods of cash pressure. It is called rolling because you update it every week and add a new week.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
Rolling ForecastRolling ForecastA forecast that is updated regularly and always looks the same period ahead.
Cash InflowsCash InflowsAll cash coming in: cash sales, card sales, invoice collections, transfers.
Cash OutflowsCash OutflowsAll cash going out: suppliers, salaries, rent, utilities, taxes, loan instalments.
COGSCost of Goods SoldHere: what you pay suppliers for goods and materials.
ARAccounts ReceivableAmounts you sold on credit and are waiting to collect from customers.
Card/Network salesCard SalesSales paid by payment card; count them when the money actually reaches your account.
Minimum Cash ReserveMinimum Cash ReserveThe lowest balance you always want to keep for emergencies.
Cash DeficitCash Deficit (liquidity gap)A week that ends with a negative balance, meaning payments exceed available cash.
Net ChangeNet ChangeInflows minus outflows during the week.
Carry forwardCarry ForwardThe week's ending balance becomes the next week's beginning balance.

Before you start

  • Choose the currency in Currency: and type the Entity Name:; both appear in the reports.
  • Gather: your current bank and cash balance, the average weekly receipts by type, and your weekly obligations.
  • Convert monthly obligations to weekly: divide the monthly amount by about 4.33 (for example, monthly rent of 21650 ÷ 4.33 = 5000 per week).

Filling in the data step by step

All amounts are weekly, in the selected currency, and cannot be negative. Growth rates are typed as percentages: 2 means 2% per week.

Opening Cash Balance & Minimum Threshold

FieldWhat to enterExample
Opening Cash Balance (Week 1)Total cash on hand and in the bank right now.100000
Minimum Cash ReserveThe lowest balance you do not want to fall below.20000

Weekly Cash Inflows

FieldWhat to enterExample
Weekly Cash SalesAverage sales received in cash each week.30000
Weekly Card/Network SalesCard sales that reach your account each week.20000
Weekly AR CollectionWhat you expect to collect from credit customers each week.15000
Weekly Inflow Growth (%)Weekly compound growth for all inflows; negative values mean a decline. 0 keeps them flat.0
Other Weekly InflowsAny other regular receipts (partner funding, other income).0

Weekly Cash Outflows

FieldWhat to enterExample
Weekly Supplier Payments (COGS)What you pay suppliers each week.18000
Weekly SalariesMonthly payroll ÷ about 4.33.15000
Weekly RentMonthly rent ÷ about 4.33.5000
Weekly UtilitiesAverage weekly electricity, water and internet bills.2000
Weekly TaxesTaxes due, spread over the weeks.1500
Weekly Loan InstallmentsLoan instalments spread over the weeks.3000
Other Weekly OutflowsAny other regular payments.1000
Weekly Outflow Growth (%)Weekly compound growth for variable outflows only (suppliers, payroll, utilities, other); rent, loan payments and taxes stay fixed by contract. 0 keeps them flat.0

Then click Run 13-Week Cash Forecast.

How the results are calculated

  • Growth factor for week w: Inflow factor = (1 + inflow growth ÷ 100)^(w − 1), and the same for outflows. Week 1 has no growth.
  • Inflows = (cash sales + card sales + AR collection + other inflows) × inflow factor
  • Outflows = (suppliers + salaries + utilities + other) × outflow factor + rent + taxes + loan (fixed contractual items do not grow).
  • Net Change = Inflows − Outflows
  • Ending Balance = Beginning Balance + Net Change, carried forward as the next week's beginning balance.
  • Weekly status: ending balance below zero: Cash Deficit; zero to below the minimum reserve: Below Minimum; otherwise: Healthy.
  • Minimum Balance = the lowest of the opening balance and all weekly ending balances.

How to read the results

  • Cards: Opening Balance, Total Inflows, Total Outflows, Net Cash Change (green if positive), Week 13 Ending Balance with its status, Minimum Balance, and Deficit Weeks out of 13.
  • Alerts: an urgent warning with the number of negative-balance weeks and immediate actions to take, a warning with the number of weeks below the minimum reserve, or an Excellent message if all 13 weeks are healthy.
  • Chart: a line of each week's ending balance with green (healthy), yellow (below minimum) or red (deficit) points, plus dashed lines for the minimum threshold and zero.
  • Detailed table: for each week, the opening balance, the inflow and outflow details and totals, net change, closing balance and status. Red rows = cash deficit; yellow rows = below the minimum threshold. Other inflows and other outflows have their own columns in the table and Excel, so the columns add up to the totals.

Export

  • Full Word Export (blue button): a report with an executive summary (opening balance, totals, net change, week 13 balance, minimum balance, deficit weeks and below-minimum weeks), the chart image, and a condensed weekly forecast table.
  • Full Excel Export (green button): a workbook with 3 sheets: Cover Page, Weekly Forecast (detailed table), Chart.

Run the forecast before exporting.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Do not enter monthly figures in weekly fields; this is the most common error and distorts the results.
  • Use actual cash timing: card sales count when they reach the account, credit invoices when they are actually collected.
  • Growth compounds weekly; 2% per week means about 27% higher in week 13 than in week 1, so use small rates.
  • When a red week appears: defer non-urgent payments, speed up collections, or arrange short-term financing before that week.
  • Update the forecast every week with actual figures to keep it accurate.

Extra help

name: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR)
content:
What is this tool and when should you use it?

It calculates the Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of an investment, sales or any value between a start point and an end point, in two forms: nominal (at current prices) and real (after removing the effect of inflation on purchasing power).

It answers the question: by what percentage did the value grow per year on average, and did that growth really beat inflation? You can also compare two investments (A and B) to see which performed better.

Use it to evaluate a past investment, compare sales growth across periods, or choose between two opportunities with different durations.

Terms and abbreviations

Abbreviation/TermFull namePlain meaning
CAGRCompound Annual Growth RateThe constant yearly rate that, repeated every year, takes the initial value to the final value.
Nominal CAGRNominal Compound Annual Growth RateGrowth at current prices, ignoring inflation.
Real CAGRReal Compound Annual Growth RateGrowth after removing inflation, i.e. growth in actual purchasing power.
nNumber of YearsThe length of the period between the initial and final values.
Fisher equationFisher EquationThe formula that converts a nominal rate into a real rate by dividing by (1 + inflation).
Purchasing powerPurchasing PowerHow much money can buy; it falls as prices rise.
Doubling timeDoubling TimeThe number of years needed for the value to double at the calculated rate.
Rule of 72Rule of 72A quick estimate of doubling time: 72 ÷ the growth percentage.
Simple growthSimple GrowthGrowth spread evenly over the years with no compounding.

Before you start

  • Choose the currency in Currency: and type the Entity Name:; both appear in the reports.
  • Prepare the value at the start and end of the period in the same currency, the number of years between them, and the average annual inflation over the period.

Filling in the data step by step

Basic Inputs

FieldWhat to enterExample
Initial ValueThe investment or sales value at the start of the period; must be greater than zero.100000
Final ValueThe value at the end of the period; greater than zero.250000
Number of Years (n)Full years between the two values (whole number, at least 1).5

Inflation (Optional — for Real CAGR)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Average Annual Inflation Rate (%)Average yearly inflation over the period as a percentage (10 means 10%, not 0.10). With 0, Real CAGR equals Nominal CAGR.10

Compare Two Investments (Optional)

FieldWhat to enterExample
Investment (B): Initial ValueStarting value of the second investment. The B fields are empty by default; leave them empty if you do not want a comparison.150000
Investment (B): Final ValueEnding value of the second investment.280000
Years (B)Duration of the second investment in years; it can differ from A.5

Then click Calculate Nominal & Real CAGR. If any basic value is zero or negative, a message asks for values greater than zero.

How the results are calculated

  • Nominal CAGR = (Final Value ÷ Initial Value)^(1 ÷ n) − 1
  • Real CAGR = (1 + Nominal CAGR) ÷ (1 + Inflation ÷ 100) − 1 (Fisher equation).
  • Total Nominal Growth % = (Final − Initial) ÷ Initial × 100, and Simple Annual Growth = Total Growth ÷ n.
  • Real Final Value = Final Value ÷ (1 + Inflation)^n (in start-year purchasing power).
  • Total Real Growth % = (Real Final − Initial) ÷ Initial × 100.
  • Purchasing Power Loss % = (Final − Real Final) ÷ Final × 100.
  • Doubling Time = ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + CAGR) for nominal and real; ∞ is shown if the rate is zero or negative. Rule of 72 = 72 ÷ (CAGR × 100).
  • Year-by-year table: compound value = Initial × (1 + CAGR)^year, real value uses the real rate, simple value = Initial + (Final − Initial) × year ÷ n.
  • The comparison is calculated only if all three B values are greater than zero; difference = A rate − B rate, and the winner is the higher rate.

How to read the results

Nominal CAGRRating
Above 15%Excellent Growth
Above 7% up to 15%Good Growth
Above 0% up to 7%Weak Growth
Exactly 0%Flat
Below 0%Decline
Real CAGRRating
Above 10%Excellent Real Growth
Above 3% up to 10%Good Real Growth
Above 0% up to 3%Weak Real Growth
Exactly 0%Flat (Real)
Below 0%Losing Purchasing Power
  • Key Performance Indicators: Nominal and Real CAGR with their ratings, Assumed Inflation with Beat Inflation if Real CAGR is above zero (otherwise Did Not Beat Inflation), Total Nominal Growth, Total Real Growth, and Purchasing Power Loss.
  • CAGR − Simple Average: the gap in percentage points between CAGR and simple annual growth. For positive growth CAGR is always less than or equal to the simple average mathematically, so a negative value means the simple average overstates growth. Example: 100,000 → 250,000 over 5 years: CAGR = 20.11%, simple average 30%, gap −9.89 points.

Tips and common mistakes

  • Enter inflation as a percentage: 10, not 0.10.
  • CAGR does not show volatility within the period; it is a compound average between two points only.
  • With positive growth, CAGR is usually lower than simple annual growth, so do not compare a compound rate with a simple rate.
  • Use the same currency at start and end, and do not add extra contributions to the final value without accounting for them.
  • When comparing investments of different lengths, CAGR is the fair measure because it is annual.
  • A negative Real CAGR means your investment is losing purchasing power even though it grows nominally.
